records.english: The purpose of the preceding remark is to reject a distinction made by certain scholars: if the preface was written before composing the book, “this” supposedly refers to meanings arranged mentally; if written afterward, it supposedly refers to things existing externally. The basis of the response can be understood from the earlier analysis of what a demonstrative indicates. The glossator nevertheless suggests that the rejection is not entirely beyond scrutiny, and asks the reader to reflect.
records.editorial: Explicit hesitation in the source; not an unequivocal endorsement of either branch.
records.revision: Stage107d source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو بعده
records.english:
Many writers use aw after sawāʾ (“it is equal whether ... or ...”), but a number of grammarians prohibit this and insist on am. Abū ʿAlī argues that aw signifies just one of the alternatives: “Whether I stand or sit, it is equal to me” would then assert equality concerning an unspecified *one*, whereas equality must concern *both*. Ibn Hishām follows him and describes al-Jawharī's example using aw as an inadvertence; he also treats a Qurʾānic reading using aw in that construction as unusual.

The glossator contends that the prohibition depends on a particular parsing. If sawāʾ is an advanced predicate and the two alternatives constitute a later subject, the supposed difficulty may appear. But al-Raḍī offers another analysis: sawāʾ is the predicate of an understood subject, such as “the two matters are equal to me.” The following interrogative clauses explicate the two matters and can be construed conditionally: “If I stand or if I sit, the two states are equal to me.” On that analysis both am and aw are possible, because the equal status of the two situations was already established by the suppressed nominal construction.

The objection can be turned against the restrictive analysis itself: am, no less than aw, can identify one among alternatives. If that alone made the sentence defective, the version with am would also fail. What matters is the syntactic explanation of the expression as a whole, not merely the lexical signification of its connective. The writer regards the second explanation as the more satisfactory.
records.editorial: Explicit disagreement between Abū ʿAlī, Ibn Hishām and al-Raḍī is the substance of the passage.
records.revision: Stage107d source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Jalāl al-Dīn al-Dawwānī (source signature)
records.arabicLemma: قوله إذ لا وجود للألفاظ ولا للمعاني في الخارج
records.english:
The statement that neither ordered words nor their meanings exist externally calls into question an earlier proposal: if a preface is composed after the treatise has been written, its “this” could point to the now-existing book rather than merely to contents in the mind. What exists externally in that case is a particular collection of *graphic marks*, not the universal words or intelligible meanings as such. Yet it would be awkward to call those marks, considered just as marks, “the utmost refinement of speech.” One could treat the marks metonymically, naming the signifying object by the thing signified; but that still requires qualification.

The present demonstrative is not meant to designate merely the particular unique written copy while excluding another copy that conveys the same linguistic and intellectual content. It denotes a type of ordered discourse, whether found in this physical copy or another sharing its significant structure. Such a universal type is not present externally as a single immediately observable thing. Accordingly, even when an actual written copy lies before the author, the referent of the title and demonstrative is primarily mentally conceived. This provides a reason for treating titles of books as names of kinds rather than merely the proper names of individual physical codices.
records.editorial: Source is attributed to Dawwānī; argument distinguishes token document vs kind rather than asserting that no spoken or written marks exist externally.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الكلام اللفظي ما يتلفظ به الإنسان والكلام النفسي
records.english:
Verbal speech (kalām lafẓī) is what a person actually articulates. Mental speech (kalām nafsī) is what a person conceives inwardly and in accordance with which spoken words may then be produced. For example, “Zayd is standing” may be considered as outwardly uttered words, while the mental representation or judgment corresponding to them is called mental speech. The source also describes the mind's organized counterpart of the uttered statement as corresponding to that external expression.

The names “verbal speech” and “mental speech” are intelligible with reference to these two sides. The words do not, merely by themselves, settle the deeper theological debate over whether mental speech is a distinct eternal divine attribute or a created psychological act; that would require the respective kalām context rather than assuming the same technical use throughout.
records.editorial: Note crosses Q153–154. Short working rendition; the published searchable text's precise assertion of correspondence and syntax requires photo check.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله حمله على هذا
records.english: The purpose of the proposed parsing is to rescue the author's apparently problematic predication. In literal terms an abstract meaning such as “refinement” cannot be predicated directly of a concrete object such as a particular book, just as was explained previously in connection with “He sent him as guidance.” Here the principal commentator proposes either emphatic figurative predication or the supply of an omitted predicate. He does not treat the abstract noun as a passive participle, although he had earlier allowed a verbal noun to stand for an active participle: the genitive combination with “speech” makes such an analysis less straightforward. One might still argue for an adjective–substantive construction, but that is not the chosen account. Other possible resolutions of abstract-to-concrete predication were already described earlier and remain conceptually available.
records.editorial: The authorial hierarchy is T matn → Y commentary → H gloss; this is an H speaker reconstructing Y's repair of T wording.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله أما على المبالغة
records.english:
There is an apparent mismatch in declaring “this book is the utmost refinement of speech”: the book is a concrete item whereas “refinement” (tahdhīb) is an action or abstract quality, and an abstract cannot literally be predicated of a concrete individual. The commentator's first solution is rhetorical intensification: the book is identified with refinement itself by an emphatic metaphor, as in “Zayd is justice.” On one explanation the abstract predicate bears no independent reference to the subject, though the Kufan grammatical tradition may instead analyse a verbal noun as derived and therefore capable of carrying a pronominal relation while receiving a more literal predication.

A second solution supplies an adjective or implied predicate: “this book is refined.” There are several possible reconstructions of the original emphatic verbal expression. The governing verb of an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) may have been omitted, the cognate accusative placed in its position, and a modifier then substituted in its turn. One could understand, for example, “this book was refined with the utmost refinement,” with successive ellipses. Another possibility inserts an omitted genitive: “the composition of this book is the utmost refinement of discourse.” A further approach understands “refinement” as “refined discourse,” treating the verbal noun as passive in sense and making the genitive relation explanatory.

An objection closes the discussion. If refinement means removing defects and superfluous material, how can this particular book be described as pure refinement when, as the glossator admits, it contains certain matters that might be judged surplus? The issue will recur later. This objection is not by itself a complete independent textual proof that the author wrote any particular surplus clause.
records.editorial: The substantive alternatives are rendered; some intermediate nominal ellipses need line-by-line Arabic pairing during later manuscript collation.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الأظهر أنه على صيغة اسم المفعول
records.english: The more apparent reading is the passive-participle form. An active-participle reading is also grammatically possible, but it is less natural in this setting.
records.editorial: A short note about vocalisation; no manuscript witness has been independently checked.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فصار تقدير الكلام هذا الكلام غاية التهذيب
records.english: The underlying formulation consequently becomes “this discourse is the utmost refinement.” A lām that might have connected the terms is omitted, and a genitive relationship takes its place, both to specify the intended meaning and to preserve the rhymed cadence (sajʿ). The expression that would have described the demonstrative “this” can then be suppressed, since the remaining words make clear which discourse is intended.
records.editorial: The phrase combines an ellipsis hypothesis with a rhetorical explanation; neither is an observed manuscript variant.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله على طريقة مجاز الحذف
records.english:
The author explains in his commentary on the Talkhīṣ that a word may be called figurative not only because its ordinary meaning is transferred, but also because the grammatical construction of the sentence changes through an omitted or added expression. As examples of omission he cites Qurʾānic wording conventionally understood as “the command of your Lord came” or “ask the people of the town.” In the latter case one asks the inhabitants, not the buildings—though God's power to make buildings speak is not denied. As an example of an additional expression he cites “There is nothing like unto His likeness,” whose intended denial is that nothing is like God, not merely that nothing resembles a second likeness distinct from Him.

The construction under discussion belongs to the first category: a phrase has been left unspoken. The reason for positing it is that without a supplied expression the surface predication would be unsuitable. This is an interpretive argument from grammatical coherence, not independent evidence of a physically omitted manuscript word.
records.editorial: Examples concern the historical theory of majāz al-ḥadhf; precise theological implications must remain source-attributed.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, reporting al-Dawwānī on the ending
records.arabicLemma: فإن التحرير هو البيان الخالي عن الحشو والزوائد
records.english:
Taḥrīr is clarification or explanation freed from unnecessary padding and surplus expressions. Bayān is broader: it can designate explanation whether or not it meets that standard. Taḥrīr can also refer specifically to setting out an intended meaning in writing, just as taqrīr can refer to presenting it in articulate exposition. This lexical distinction was perhaps not pursued by the principal commentator because it adds relatively little to the present reasoning.

The following preposition “in” expresses a figurative containment. Broad conceptual inclusion is likened to the spatial inclusion of something in a vessel, and the particle ordinarily signifying physical location is transferred to the conceptual relation. Such a figurative container cannot be assumed to reveal a new literal physical object. A source note ascribed to al-Dawwānī supplies a formulation of the first explanation at the beginning of the next printed page.
records.editorial: First-pass across Q154→155; precise last-clause attribution and what 'الأول' resumes need photograph-assisted check.
records.revision: Stage107e source-linked first-pass English; Arabic locator only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله والمنطق آلة قانونية
records.english:
On “logic is a rule-governed instrument”: an instrument is an intermediary between an agent and the thing affected by the agent, through which the agent's effect reaches its recipient—like the pen between the writer and what is written. The word qānūn is said to come from Greek or Syriac, originally used for a ruling line in writing. In technical usage a canon is a universal proposition from which rulings concerning its subject's particular cases are learned. The term will be discussed in greater detail later. Thinking is the arrangement of known matters to obtain matters not yet known.

Logic is called an *instrument* because it mediates between the rational power and the theoretical objects it seeks to acquire. It is called *rule-governed* because its problems formulate universal rules by which judgments concerning particular instances become known. For example, if one knows the rule that a universal affirmative converts to a particular affirmative, one can infer from “Every human is an animal” that “Some animal is human.” This example presupposes the intended existential context; it does not automatically settle the modern empty-domain interpretation of a universal proposition.

The definition ascribes protection from error to the *observance* of logical rules. Possessing the discipline itself does not confer infallibility: otherwise anyone trained in logic would never err, whereas one can plainly make mistakes by neglecting the art and failing to apply its precepts.

The definition's elements can now be distinguished. “Instrument” functions like a genus; “rule-governed” like a more remote differentia, excluding the particular tools used by craftsmen; and its final qualification like a nearer differentia, distinguishing logic from other rule-governed studies that preserve correctness in speech rather than in thinking—for instance grammar and morphology.

Strictly, however, the definition is a *rasm* (descriptive definition), not a *ḥadd* (essential definition). An essential definition uses intrinsic constituents. Logic's instrumentality is relational to other disciplines, not something constituting its essence considered in isolation. Error-prevention is also its end, which is extrinsic to the thing defined; defining a science through its purpose is therefore descriptive.

An objection is that logic can be instrumental in relation to logic itself: one logical proposition is used to establish another. The initial answer says that such use occurs between distinct parts, rather than the entire science being instrumental to itself; to make instrumentality essential to the whole, one would need each problem to be instrumental to itself. The glossator suggests that the reply is more elaborate than necessary. Even if logic has some reflexive uses, its instrumental relation to another discipline is enough to show that the relationship is not intrinsic to logic as such. An essential attribute must belong to a thing through what it is, not merely through comparison with something else.
records.editorial: Working source-based full first-pass of note104 on instrumentality, qānūn, observance, rasm/ḥadd, reflective use. Arabic locator only; original printed page and internal quotations require photo collation.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي واجب الوجود والمعاد هو في اللغة بمعنى الرجوع
records.english: The first expression means “the Necessary Existent.” As for maʿād, its linguistic meaning is returning; in the present theological discussion it signifies the soul's return to the body after its separation from it. This is an explanation of the particular theological use of the term, not a general dictionary claim that every occurrence of maʿād means bodily resurrection.
records.editorial: Short note distinguishes lexical from doctrinal usage.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله على نهج قانون الإسلام
records.english:
On “according to the rule or method of Islam”: this qualification distinguishes kalām from philosophical inquiry, since philosophers also investigate the conditions of the first principle and the return, yet do not formally require their conclusions to conform to the religious law of Islam as a condition of the inquiry.

The intended exclusion should not be exaggerated. The point is that philosophical investigation does not *make conformity to the revealed law a formal criterion*, not that it positively requires its findings to *contradict* that law. Were one to assume the latter, a philosopher who accepts philosophy would, simply by that fact, be obliged to adopt positions contrary to the purified religious law and thus be judged an unbeliever; that does not follow from the methodological distinction. **Not taking a property into account is logically different from taking its absence into account.** The negative qualification on the criterion is not a positive criterion of nonconformity.
records.editorial: Important contrast between the absence of a formal constraint and a positive contradictory constraint; not a global judgment on philosophers' religious status.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الظاهر من كلامه أن العامل في المعطوف
records.english:
The apparent assumption is that the governor of the coordinated expression is the same governor that acts on the first expression, operating through the coordinating particle; this is the majority position and is regarded here as sound. Others assign the grammatical operation directly to the coordinating particle, while yet others posit an implicit governor after it. A further view describes the coordinated word as governed by the word with which it is coordinated; arguments can be found for this account as well.

One might instead coordinate the disputed expression with “refinement” (taḥrīr), as reported from al-Dawwānī. The whole would then mean that the work represents the utmost refinement of discourse in bringing the intended objectives nearer—that is, arranging an argument so that the desired conclusion follows. The glossator finds that construction closer to the superficial wording but less fitting to the intended sense, and suggests that this is why the principal commentator does not examine it.
records.editorial: Speaker signatures and exactly which coordination is under discussion need the printed column or immediately preceding principal lemma.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, p.11 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله والحمل أي حمل قوله غاية تقريب المرام
records.english: “Predication” here means predicating “the utmost approximation of the intended aim” of the demonstrative “this.” It may be understood as emphatic figurative predication, just as an abstract source is predicated of a concrete person in “Zayd is justice.” Alternatively a predicate of the subject has been omitted, and the phrase “the utmost approximation of the intended aim” functions as a cognate accusative raised, as it were, into the predicate's position after the omission. The underlying wording is “This discourse brings the intended purpose nearer to the utmost degree.” The same grammatical possibilities were already discussed for “This is the utmost refinement of speech.”
records.editorial: Quoted al-Taqrīb author not principal al-Yazdī; first-pass reconstruction of alternative syntactic analyses.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يخفى أن الأولى أن يقرأ مقرب
records.english: The expression muqarrib (“one that brings near”) is preferably read as an active participle, as al-Dawwānī expressly maintains. A passive-participle reading can also be admitted, but it is the less likely alternative in this context.
records.editorial: Reading preference reported by glossator; no photographed manuscript reading certified.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يعني أن كلمة من لبيان الجنس
records.english:
The preposition min is understood as explicating a genus or class (bayān al-jins). It occurs especially often after the indefinite expressions mā and mahmā because of their breadth and ambiguity, as in Qurʾānic constructions equivalent to “whatever verse We abrogate” and “whatever sign you bring us.” Yet it can also follow other words, as in the Qurʾānic prohibition concerning the abomination of idols.

The prepositional phrase functions as a circumstantial adjunct (ḥāl) and is therefore in the accusative position in syntactic analysis. One can reconstruct it with an understood “being from the establishment of the doctrines of Islam.” The same applies to analogous constructions.

Certain grammarians reject the category of explanatory min altogether. On their approach, this particular min is construed partitively instead. The difference between a genus-explaining and a partitive reading remains an interpretive alternative rather than one settled by the mere appearance of the preposition.
records.editorial: Two grammatical schools' analyses retained; Qurʾānic examples are text-specific and need verse-by-verse cross-check.
records.revision: Stage107f first-pass H gloss translation; Arabic lemma only

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله والإضافة في عقائد الإسلام بيانية
records.english:
On the assertion that the genitive construction in “the doctrines of Islam” (ʿaqāʾid al-Islām) is explanatory: the conventional account of semantic genitive constructions usually reduces them to the meanings of lām (belonging, specification) or, less commonly, fī (containment in a time or place). To determine which applies, one first considers how the extensions of the two terms are related. The standard four logical relations are equality, complete separation, inclusion of one under the other, and overlap without complete inclusion.

If the two terms are coextensive, the genitive relation is normally inadmissible unless the terms are interpreted in a way that changes their relation into one of the other three classes. If they are wholly separate, one must ask whether a meaningful relation exists at all. Without one, a genitive construction cannot be justified. With one, the specific relation governs its interpretation. If the second term denotes the time or place containing the first, as in “the stratagem of night,” “the waiting of four months,” or “the inhabitants of the prison,” the construction can mean “in.” Otherwise it is ordinarily understood in terms of lām, covering numerous relations: a place designated for an action, a person's limb or speech, something owned, something associated with a person, and kinship.

In a relation of complete inclusion, the construction may be impossible as ordinarily stated if the second term is broader and the first denotes an instance not properly expressible by that genitive form; but if a suitable reinterpretation can be made, the familiar lām construction returns. Conversely, a first term and a more restricted second can be combined as “Sunday's day,” “the science of jurisprudence,” or “the arāk tree,” according to their conceptual functions. Where the terms overlap, a genitive meaning “from” may arise if the second designates the material or origin of the first; otherwise lām remains available.

Apply this to “beliefs of Islam.” If “Islam” is taken as the beliefs themselves, their conceptual relation to the doctrines requires careful analysis. The glossator argues that, under the stated general rules, lām would be the expected interpretation. He understands the principal commentator's proposed explanatory construction as relying on another scholar's judgment that the semantic sense is clearer if an implicit “from” is made explicit. But he objects that this conflicts with the grammatical distribution just rehearsed, calling it a departure from the received agreement.

The discussion is thus not merely about theological ownership. It tests a genitive phrase against a taxonomy of relations between extensions, moving from general logic of universals to a choice among grammatical readings. The accusation of consensus violation belongs to this particular glossator, not to a newly established historical consensus.
records.editorial: Long cross-page first-pass translation of Q156–157. Several of the author's intermediate examples are interpreted conceptually; the exact printed taxonomic divisions should be photographically checked.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm; following passage by Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī separate
records.arabicLemma: قوله وإن كان عبارة عن مجموع الإقرار باللسان
records.english:
If “Islam” is understood as the composite of verbal profession and its associated acknowledgment, the discussion touches the relationship between Islam and faith (īmān). One report from al-Riḍā is cited as support for treating their meanings as equivalent. By contrast, a view reported from the Shaykh of the school makes faith more comprehensive: its essence is the heart's assent while verbal profession is taken into account in its manifestation.

The glossator supports the inward conception by lexical usage. Īmān in ordinary Arabic signifies accepting or believing someone's statement. The Qurʾānic speech of Joseph's brothers—“You would not believe us”—uses the word in the sense of accepting testimony; another Qurʾānic example speaks of believing in al-jibt and al-ṭāghūt. In colloquial speech too, people say that someone believes or does not believe a particular account. There is no warrant for presuming that religious usage has transferred the word to an altogether different primary signification unless evidence for that transfer is produced.

An objection says that one cannot conventionally recognize inward assent without speech, so outward articulation must be part of the concept of faith. The reply is that an inward conviction may indeed exist in someone unable to speak, or someone who remains silent. The conclusion drawn is that the reality of faith is inward assent, while speech and bodily action are necessary for its appearance and social recognition.
records.editorial: Note112 ends at signature (ʿAbd al-Raḥīm). A much longer quotation explicitly introduced as 'Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī said in some marginalia' follows and continues to Q158. It is stored separately, not counted as note113.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī in separate H gloss quoted after HWN-112, Q157–158
unnumberedFollowing.ar: اعلم أن الإسلام على ما يستفاد من الأخبار هو الإقرار باللسان
unnumberedFollowing.en: A separately quoted writer argues that Islam in its broad legal sense consists in professing that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is His messenger, whether or not inward assent and corresponding action accompany the profession. Islam is therefore broader in extension than faith. He adduces a reported dialogue with Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq distinguishing the outward Muslim status—on which life is protected and the rules of marriage and inheritance operate—from faith as a state established inwardly and shown through righteous action. On that account faith entails Islam in outward practice, whereas outward Islam does not entail inward faith. Qurʾān 49:14, which tells certain desert Arabs to say “We have submitted” rather than “We have believed,” is cited as support. The writer then distinguishes bare verbal acknowledgment from the fuller sense of Islam in which it is accompanied by heartfelt belief and action. This is the cited Imāmī account, including its own assessment of other opinions; no independent authentication of the reported narration has been performed.

records.speaker: Printed siglum M–B, unidentified
records.arabicLemma: بفتح الجيم القلب الذي هو المراد ههنا
records.english:
With fatḥa on the jīm, janān means the heart; it is given that designation because the heart is concealed within the breast. Another suggested explanation derives the name from the heart's gathering or retaining impressions, though the glossator regards this as remote. The word belongs to the root j-n-n, which conveys covering, hiding or being concealed. Qurʾānic usage describes unborn children (ajinna) within their mothers, similarly hidden from view.

The same root yields jinn, beings described in the inherited lexicon as hidden from ordinary vision; a traditional definition says they may assume different forms. The author distinguishes this from a theological demonstration of the existence or character of these beings. The root also supplies forms denoting darkness or being covered, including the Qurʾānic expression about night covering Abraham.

The garden, janna, takes its name from trees and foliage which shelter and cover the ground; hence the plural jannāt and scriptural descriptions of gardens underneath which rivers flow. With a different vocalisation, junna means a covering or shield: related forms describe a protection against weapons. The lexical collection unites these senses through concealment but does not make them synonymous in every context.
records.editorial: Multiple homographic j-n-n words require exact vowelling. Manuscript signature M–B is not independently identified; metaphysical definition of jinn is lexicographic report, not scientifically established.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله فالإضافة لامية
records.english: The genitive construction is to be interpreted as involving lām because the first and second terms are distinct in extension. This is obvious under the second analysis. Under the first it follows from the fact that a composite differs from its constituent parts: the medicinal preparation sakanjabīn is not identical with the vinegar and honey of which it is composed. Hence the suggestion that, on this reading, “beliefs” would simply be universally broader than “Islam” is not to be accepted.
records.editorial: Short full digitally searchable Arabic working transcription; authorial response is to the previous categorical/genitive analysis, not an independent empirical claim.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English
records.arabicFullText: قوله فالإضافة لامية : لمكان التباين بين المضاف والمضاف اليه اما على الثاني فظاهر واما على الأول فلضرورة ان المركب يباين الاجزاء كما ترى في السكنجبين بالنسبة إلى الخل والعسل فما توهم من أن العقائد أعم منه مطلقا بهذا المعنى فليس مما يلتفت اليه .

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ويحتمل التجوز في الإسناد
records.english:
Figurative attribution (majāz fī al-isnād) occurs when an action or description is predicated of something other than its proper bearer, as in “his day fasted,” “the river ran” or “the waterspout flowed.” Here the book is said to provide “insight” (tabṣira), even though strictly it is the action or intellectual work of the book's author—and, derivatively, the book's function—that gives insight.

One can understand the phrase as an intensified predication, or assume an omitted noun: “I made it a possessor of insight” or “I made its condition and function a source of insight.” The same kind of reconstruction applies to the subsequent statement that the book is “a reminder” (tadhkira). The examples clarify a distinction between a property in the subject literally and an effect or instrument attributed to it by association.
records.editorial: Full digitally searchable Arabic working transcription from p158, unverified against original photograph.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English
records.arabicFullText: قوله ويحتمل التجوز في الاسناد : بان يجعل الحمد على سبيل المبالغة كما مر مرارا . والتجوز في الاسناد هو اسناد الشئ إلى غير ما هو له مثل « صام نهاره » و « جرى النهر » و « سال الميزاب » وهنا اسناد التبصرة إلى الضمير من هذا القبيل فان الأصل فيه ان يسند إلى فعل الكتاب وشأنه بل فعل المصنّف أو شأنه ، هذا . ويحتمل ان يكون على تقدير المضاف اما قبل التبصرة اى جعلته ذا تبصرة أو قبل الضمير ، اى : جعلت شأنه وحاله تبصرة ، وقس على هذا قوله تذكرة .

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يعني أن فاعل الإفهام ومفعوله كلاهما محذوف
records.english:
Both the agent and object of the action of causing understanding (ifhām) have been omitted. Two reconstructions are possible: the teacher or another person could be the agent and the person described by the relative expression its recipient, or conversely the person so described could be the one who imparts understanding and someone else its recipient.

On the second interpretation, there is a straightforward parallel for the definite article standing in place of a suppressed third-person pronoun, as in Qurʾānic or other established constructions. The first interpretation raises a more technical objection: replacement by the definite article is commonly explained when the thing suppressed is pronominal, whereas here it might replace a noun that would otherwise be overt.

The reply is twofold. First, the case need not be analysed as suppression followed by substitution: a noun or pronoun can simply be suppressed on the strength of a contextual indication, and that licence is more general. Second, even granting that it is a case of replacement, there is no proof that substitution by the definite article is restricted to absent third-person pronouns; it may extend to ordinary nouns and forms referring to the speaker or listener.

A reported Qurʾānic interpretation from al-Zamakhsharī and a grammatical discussion from Abū Shāma are adduced in the continuation, showing that expressions with generic overt forms can carry an implicitly particular reference. Frequency of such a construction does not establish that it is exclusive.
records.editorial: Crosses p158→159 and includes reports from earlier authors. Source-text full Arabic still to be collated and separately attributed.
records.revision: Stage108 first-pass source-backed H numbered-note English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو تفهيمه للغير
records.english:
The words “or his giving understanding to another” mean his teaching that person. Here the disjunction aw need not assert that just one of the two possibilities holds; it can rule out the absence of both. The book may furnish insight both to the learner and to the teacher: one can read the preface as saying that the book assists a person seeking understanding in a context of imparting knowledge, whether that person is teaching another or being instructed by another.

A less expansive reading follows what is normally apparent: the work functions as an aid to one of these, and most naturally to the learner. This may explain why the principal commentator begins from the learner's perspective. The difference is between an exclusive alternative and an inclusive pair of possibilities, not two entirely different meanings of “insight.”
records.editorial: Tracks disjunction as māniʿ al-khulūw, allowing both branches; voice requires printed signature control.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو متعلق بيتذكر
records.english:
The prepositional expression may be an adverbial predicate (ẓarf mustaqarr) attached to a suppressed verb and functioning as a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of yatadhakkar (“he takes heed”). The subject is the implicit pronoun referring back to “whoever” in the relative expression. The underlying sense would be that the book was made a reminder for whoever wishes to recollect, *being among those who possess understanding*.

Alternatively the expression may be an ordinary adjunct (ẓarf laghw) directly governed by yatadhakkar. To make that latter construction semantically appropriate the commentator adds an implied sense of taking or learning. The mere verb “take heed” does not normally take the particular preposition min in the required manner, but a broader meaning of “take [knowledge] from” or “learn from” makes the link intelligible.

This is an example of taḍmīn, semantic inclusion: the overt verb retains its own central meaning while also allowing a closely related second verb to be understood, as indicated by the preposition appropriate to the second. One can make the overt verb primary and the implied sense subsidiary, or invert the priority. The glossator compares other expressions in learned introductions, such as “I arranged it according to such-and-such,” and commentary on Ibn al-Ḥājib's use of a phrase containing an atypical preposition.
records.editorial: Clarifies that an apparent syntactic anomaly can reflect an intentionally included additional verbal meaning.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله هذا أيضا يحتمل الوجهين
records.english:
The expression “this too admits two interpretations” parallels the preceding discussion of the phrase “when giving understanding.” The description “among the people of understanding” can describe the teacher if it is a predicative circumstantial expression, or the learner if it is directly attached to “take heed” by the semantic inclusion just explained.

That is the ordinary explanation. Yet the first construction also permits one to describe the learner as possessing understanding, so the opposition is not logically exhaustive. The reading preferred on contextual grounds remains the first, but it should not be transformed into a claim that the rival referent is impossible.
records.editorial: Later gloss distinguishes grammatical possibility from interpretive preference.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: السِّيُّ بالتشديد وقد يخفف
records.english: The word siyy is pronounced with a doubled final consonant, although lighter pronunciations are attested, including in expressions with lā siyamā (“especially”). Its historical root is explained through the idea of equality or likeness, with an underlying wāw in some forms. When it is put into the dual, a separate genitive complement can sometimes be dispensed with, just as one may use the dual of mithl (“like, equal”) without an additional genitive expression. Examples are cited where two evils are called alike. The dual itself can supply the sense of the two corresponding terms; forming a similarly regular dual of sawāʾ is said to be rare.
records.editorial: Traditional morphology of siyy and its dialectal reduction, not independently collated against earliest lexical authorities.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī; reports Thaʿlab and al-Raḍī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وأصل سيما لا سيما حذفت لا في اللفظ
records.english:
On the remark that the original expression was lā siyamā and that lā was subsequently dropped in speech: Thaʿlab is reported to have disapproved uses of the phrase that depart from an established poetic example employing “wa-lā siyamā.” His explanation is that lā siyamā has become a set expression introducing a matter more important or more highly ranked than what preceded. For example, “Charity is recommended in Ramadan, especially in its final ten nights” says that the recommendation becomes stronger in those nights than in Ramadan generally.

If one omitted lā and said only siyamā, he argues, the word would retain its ordinary sense of likeness or equivalence. The sentence would then compare the recommendation in Ramadan with that in the final ten nights rather than emphasizing the superiority of the latter.

But this reason establishes at most that the negative particle must be part of the interpretation—either pronounced or understood. It does not prove that the particle must always be uttered. Al-Raḍī notes that frequency of use has led to several altered forms: the expression occurs with lā omitted, and the yāʾ can be lightened with or without lā. Accordingly a linguistic argument for an underlying negative meaning should not be confused with proof that every conventional surface form must pronounce lā.
records.editorial: Cross-page reading preserves Thaʿlab's prescriptive position and a specific objection based on al-Raḍī's usage evidence.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, p.12 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله هذا أصله ثم استعمل بمعنى خصوصا
records.english: The statement that lā siyamā originally had one structure and was then used to mean “especially” does not require positing a wholly new sense. Its ordinary meaning and its idiomatic employment can be explained on one underlying account: the force of “especially this” is already implicit in saying that nothing is comparable to this case within the relevant set. The usage need not be treated as a distinct transferred meaning absent from its original composition.
records.editorial: Source attribution to the quoted al-Taqrīb, not the main author.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفيما بعده ثلاثة أوجه
records.english:
The word that follows lā siyamā can appear in three principal grammatical cases. In the genitive it is treated as the complement of siyy, while mā between them is regarded as an extra particle, comparable to expressions such as “which of the two appointed terms.” In the nominative the noun can be a predicate of an omitted subject; mā may then be interpreted as a relative pronoun whose clause is partly suppressed, or as an indefinite modified by an understood clause. This gives something like “there is no equal to that which is the most beloved son” or “to a thing which is the most beloved son.”

The genitive analysis is preferred to the nominative by some, because suppressing the beginning of a relative or adjectival clause is unusual. The nominative proposal can also require taking mā, ordinarily associated with nonrational referents, as referring to a rational person; this is controversial. Details of the vocalisation of siyy and its relation to the suppressed construction depend on the adopted parsing.

For the accusative there are again alternatives. One may posit an omitted verb “I mean,” making the following noun an object of specification, or treat it as a specification (tamyīz) when indefinite, comparable to an accusative of specification after mithl. In that interpretation mā prevents the genitive construction from operating. A further proposal analyses the phrase as an exception; critics argue that the element following the phrase is often expressly preferred rather than *excluded*. The reply is that it can be excluded from the equality suggested by the previous clause—a disconnected exception rather than removal from the subject class.

The coordinating wāw presents another difficulty for an exception reading, since one would not ordinarily say “the people came, and except Zayd” in that manner. Some answer that the entire idiom, with its variant pronunciations, has acquired a conventional force comparable to an exceptive construction. The glossator finally warns that this debate does not justify declaring the accusative impossible whenever the following noun is definite.
records.editorial: A detailed first-pass translation of the three case patterns; individual reported examples and disputed phraseology still require a manuscript-controlled syntax review.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: يعني أن فعّالا ههنا بمعنى ما يفعل به
records.english: The morphological pattern faʿʿāl in this position has the sense of an instrument: the thing by means of which an action is performed. The explanation concerns the semantic function of the derived form, not every possible occurrence of that pattern.
records.editorial: Short morphological note, source is limited to one sentence.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Uncertain voice at page seam after 124
records.arabicLemma: هذا معناه العرفي ومعناه اللغوي رباط القربة
records.english: The earlier explanation is the conventional technical meaning. In its literal lexical origin ʿiṣām means the tie or strap of a waterskin. One says ʿaṣama al-qirba when someone secures the waterskin with its fastening. The developed sense of protection is connected to the idea of holding something secure and preventing its loss.
records.editorial: A source lexeme ʿiṣām is here glossed; attribution inherited from page is not independently photo-collated.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ثم السجع في اللغة هدير الحمام
records.english:
The preceding indication of restriction does not prevent a statement from having several different reasons or rhetorical effects: multiple causal and explanatory considerations can coexist.

Sajʿ lexically denotes the cooing or repeated call of a dove and similar sounds. A poetic line is quoted addressing a dove and inviting it to coo while in hearing of Suʿād. Technically, sajʿ in prose is the agreement of the terminal members of two clauses in their final sound or letter. The term may also be applied to the final word itself insofar as it agrees with the ending of a neighbouring clause.

Thus when one says “sajʿ in prose is like qāfiya in poetry,” the comparison concerns the terminal element, not merely an abstract agreement between any two final words; the strictly relational feature is more closely associated with the operation of making the ends rhyme. In practice the pairing of prose endings may require a pause and suppression of the final case ending, hence the rule that balanced prose endings are often read with sukun at their closures.

Some scholars dislike calling the recurrent terminations of Qurʾānic verses sajʿ, both because of the word's ordinary association with the dove's call and because sacred discourse should not be classified under an inapt literary label. They prefer fawāṣil, “verse endings,” and speak of the heads of verses. The rhetorical phenomenon and the choice of a respectful technical designation should therefore be distinguished.
records.editorial: The verse, original technical definition and decorum claim belong to the glossator's cited tradition; no independent literary-critical attribution verified.
records.revision: Stage108b source-linked new H numbered note, first-pass English

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: وقيل هو ترك السعي فيما لا يسعه قدرة البشر
records.english: A further account of tawakkul (reliance on God) says that one refrains from striving in matters that lie outside the scope of human ability. One employs the appropriate *cause* or means, yet does not imagine that the effect is produced by oneself independently. The speaker adduces the well-known reported instruction, “Tie up your camel and place your trust in God.” Reliance therefore need not exclude the practical use of causes. Rather, it excludes claiming independent control over the outcome.
records.editorial: Short source note ends with Muḥammad ʿAlī's signature. The cited hadith is reported by the glossator; its authentication is not established by this translation.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.13 (reported)
records.arabicLemma: هذا معناه العرفاني لا اللغوي
records.english: That is the spiritual or gnostic meaning of tawakkul, not its basic lexical meaning. In language, tawakkul denotes relying upon a thing or person, placing confidence in it, or treating it as what one depends upon: “he relied on him” means “he counted upon him and depended on him.” The technical spiritual account may therefore be narrower and richer than the ordinary dictionary sense.
records.editorial: Quoted al-Taqrīb gloss, a separate voice from preceding Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله لما علم ضمنا
records.english:
On “since it was understood implicitly”: the particle lammā may be treated as an adverbial of time, or as a particle comparable to idh. It links the occurrence of the content of one sentence with the occurrence of another. In “when Zayd arrived, ʿAmr arrived,” those treating lammā as a particle may express the first occurrence as explanatory of the second, while those treating it as a temporal adverb assert only their simultaneity or conjunction in time, whether the two events are causally related or merely coincide.

The point of this discussion is to explain the indefinite form of muqaddima (“an introduction”) and the definite form of the two divisions of the book. Adding the definite article is not an unmotivated act: it requires a reason. The two divisions have already been referred to, at least implicitly, and can therefore be named as known; the introduction has not been introduced in the same way and remains indefinite. The first division is accordingly called *the* first division.

One objection says that the absence of a previously mentioned referent does not require an indefinite expression. The definite article can also indicate a familiar external referent or other types of definiteness. The initial explanation is therefore incomplete if it implies that prior verbal mention is the only possible ground of definition. Moreover external familiarity can single out a determinate object even where it was not previously named in speech. The order of exposition also has a purpose: the author begins with logic because that first division is preparatory to the second, theology.
records.editorial: The reported temporal-vs-causal semantics of lammā are historical grammarians' analyses, not a complete formal semantics. Source Q161 is long but one numbered gloss.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أن لما هذه تختص بالماضي
records.english:
The lammā under discussion is especially connected with past occurrences and requires two clauses, the second happening in relation to the first, as in “when he invited me, I responded.” Grammarians disagree whether it is a particle or an adverb. Among the particle analyses there are further disputes over whether it links one event's existence to the existence of another or makes one obligation follow another. Those who call it an adverb differ over its correspondence to ḥīn (“when”) or idh (“at the time when”).

Ibn Khurūf reportedly objects to calling lammā an adverb, since a person may say “when you honoured me yesterday, I honoured you today.” If the verb in the consequent governs lammā as an adverb, it seems that one verb would have to occupy two different times. The reply distinguishes the time of the act from the time of the fact's becoming established: one may understand “when it was established today that you had honoured me yesterday, I honoured you.” The source compares this with the Qurʾānic construction “If I had said it, You would have known it,” whose relevant conditional relation need not assign the two acts the same time.

This also answers an objection about the author's organisation. The expression “the first division” normally follows an explicit division into two or more parts; the writer had not previously stated a numbered table of contents. Yet he had already referred to the refinement of discourse in *logic and theology*, which indicates the two parts sufficiently for a subsequent mention of “the first division.”

The principal gloss then distinguishes why that first division is definite but the introduction is indefinite. Some take that distinction to be the whole aim of the comment, rather than a subsidiary consequence of establishing the implied division. The present glossator replies that this fails to explain the wording and the explanatory connective in the principal gloss. If the definite/indefinite contrast alone were the primary goal, a different past-tense formulation without the fāʾ would have been stylistically expected.
records.editorial: Long source note ends in Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī signature; one first-pass English reading, not photographed and not modern-modal formal proof.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.13 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله لم يحتج إلى التصريح بهذا
records.english: “He did not need to express this openly” refers to the fact that the book consists of two divisions: logic and theology. Thus the first division concerns logic. The division has already been implied, even though the formal classification was not pronounced in so many words.
records.editorial: Short quoted al-Taqrīb explanation, not original principal al-Yazdī speech.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ربما يتوهم ان هذا انما يقتضى انتفاء تعريفها بلام العهد
records.english:
An objector might say that the preceding reasoning eliminates at most the definite article of prior mention (*lām al-ʿahd al-dhikrī*). It does not prove that every type of definiteness is impossible, since the absence of one special class does not imply the absence of the entire general class.

The first reply is contextual. The author was contrasting this introduction with the first division, which was definite by virtue of having been mentioned. For that limited contrast it suffices to identify the missing ground of definiteness. A second reply appeals to the other possible readings: in this location neither universal comprehensiveness, a familiar technical introduction, quiddity considered simply as such, nor an unspecified individual instance would be suitable. Since the alternatives are contextually unavailable, the particular reason of previous mention can be cited without rehearsing the others.

The glossator clarifies the form of the objection: the proposed conclusion seems broader than the evidence, which excludes only one member of the class. He suggests two ways to restore a proper relation between evidence and conclusion. Either restrict what the conclusion itself is claiming, or treat the stated evidence as a conspicuous part of a larger argument whose remaining premises are sufficiently obvious to have been omitted.
records.editorial: Contains quotation and subsequent explanation signed by Muḥammad ʿAlī; excludes a formal logical error only under the contextual restriction made explicit.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.13 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: ليس المراد بالقسم الأول الا المسائل المنطقية
records.english:
An objection says that “the first division” simply means the questions of logic. If “logic” means those same questions, the two expressions differ only in their wording, not their referent. One cannot literally place something *in* itself merely by changing its name: a contained thing and its container must be distinct.

The principal commentary answers by distinguishing a book's title from what is titled. The “first division” may designate the heading or organized literary part, while logic denotes the discipline's subject-matter. Those are different enough for a relation of inclusion. The quoted marginal critic finds the remaining elaborate explanations unnecessary: they distinguish words, meanings, graphic inscriptions, pairwise combinations, triple combinations, acquired logical disposition, the science of all logical problems or a substantial body of them, and the problems themselves. In his judgment this enumeration mostly multiplies expressions without advancing the explanation.
records.editorial: A substantial editorial criticism from al-Taqrīb, not an agreed conclusion of the principal commentary.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يلزم اتحاد الظرف والمظروف
records.english: The objection is that the contained and the container would become identical, which is impossible for a literal relation of containment. A thing cannot contain itself in exactly the same respect in which it is contained. A different conceptual consideration or a genuinely different referent is required if the wording is to be defended.
records.editorial: One-sentence categorical distinction; later notes qualify the issue for metaphorical containment.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: يجوز ان يراد بالقسم الأول
records.english:
Most of the proposed ways of interpreting containment can be made intelligible. One exception occurs when “the first division” means the meanings of the logical propositions and “logic” means the propositions themselves. If the propositions are just those meanings, the phrase reduces to “these meanings in these meanings,” and the objection of self-containment returns.

An attempted solution says that “the first division” denotes a universal whose only instance lies in logic, so the sense would be “this universal is in this particular.” A critic regards that as contrived. Another solution treats the first division as a part of logic, because the discipline is not exhausted by the questions in this literary division. The intended relation would then be “this particular part is in the wider whole.” Such a part–whole relation is clearer than making a universal literally present inside its own single instance.
records.editorial: Reports competing resolutions of the same container/contained argument; the part–whole reading is not automatically valid if 'logic' means only exactly the same selected problems.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: وهي ثلاث صور : الالفاظ مع المعاني
records.english: The three twofold combinations mentioned are (1) expressions together with meanings, (2) expressions together with graphic inscriptions, and (3) meanings together with inscriptions. This enumerates the three pairs that can be formed from the three basic levels of a book—its verbal wording, what that wording signifies, and its written marks. The source begins the enumeration at the end of Q162 and completes its final item at the beginning of Q163.
records.editorial: Exact cross-page source boundary; a short enumerative gloss, not three new source manuscripts.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: والمنطق عبارة عن أحد معان خمسة اما الملكة
records.english:
The word malaka (“acquired disposition”) denotes a quality that has become settled so firmly in the person who possesses it that it cannot be readily removed at will. If a quality does not yet have that stability and the person can easily rid himself of it, it is called a ḥāl (“state”). This understanding of malaka is one of the common senses in which knowledge is spoken of. The glossator wonders why a particular marginal commentator on al-Muṭawwal did not include it.

A further objection concerns the familiar metaphor that expressions are the moulds of meanings. If a book or its division is treated as verbal expressions *contained in* meanings, while meanings themselves are treated as *contained in* verbal expressions, does each become both container and contained by the other?

The reply distinguishes standpoints. The “container” of words can be their *explanatory function*: expressions are arranged to disclose meanings, which may also be disclosed without those particular expressions. In that respect the work of explaining meanings provides a governing framework for the expressions. Conversely verbal expressions can be described as moulds of meanings because the understanding obtained from them expands or contracts with the expressions, and meanings are received through their formulation.

It is impossible for one and the same thing to be container and contained of itself *in the same respect* under the same literal relation. But the two descriptions here concern different relations and are partly metaphorical, so the alleged contradiction does not follow.
records.editorial: Malaka vs ḥāl and two distinct 'container' respects. Speaker ends with ʿAbd al-Raḥīm signature.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.13 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: العلم بجميع المسائل أو نفس المسائل
records.english: The difference between “knowing all the questions” and “the questions themselves” is that in the first case the questions are considered under the illumination of being known or disclosed, while in the second they are considered simply as questions in themselves, without considering their disclosure to any particular knower. The same contents are thus distinguished by whether their epistemic relation is included in the conception.
records.editorial: Quoted al-Taqrīb note distinguishes knowledge-as-disclosure from known propositions considered apart from their epistemic status.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فيحصل من ملاحظة الخمسة
records.english:
Most combinations of the seven possible referents of “the first division” and five possible meanings of “logic” can be interpreted straightforwardly. A problematic class remains where the first division is taken as meanings, either alone or combined with another element, while logic is taken as the problems themselves, whether all of them or a substantial selection. The problems themselves are those meanings. The result then seems to be “meanings are in meanings,” merely returning to the objection the explanation was supposed to escape.

One answer distinguishes the division from the whole discipline: the first division comprises only a part of logic, since not every possible logical question appears in it. Therefore a particular subset can be said to be within the wider class. But this does not solve the case where “logic” denotes only the substantial body of problems actually in the very same division; then the division is not a proper part of that body but the same thing.

Another proposed answer distinguishes unrestricted meanings from meanings of a special kind. On this reading one says in effect that the meanings of the book serve to explain this particular kind of meaning, namely logical meanings. This is compatible with the earlier restriction to specific words and meanings, the glossator says, when each statement is taken under its proper conceptual aspect. Merely considering a thing under an aspect does not bring into existence a second independent thing.
records.editorial: Source explicitly rejects a first attempted part–whole repair in the narrow case and distinguishes conceptual consideration from numerically distinct things.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.13 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: يقدر في بعضها
records.english:
Even when one of the thirty-five combinations—seven possible things meant by the first division multiplied by five possible senses of logic—has been given a formally defensible container/contained relation, one further requirement remains. The actual words must yield an idiomatic and intellectually appropriate sentence.

For example, “the words in the disposition” may avoid the strongest logical objection to containment, but it does not read naturally in the present literary construction. One should instead speak of “words *for acquiring* the disposition,” “words *for explaining* the meanings,” or “words *for attaining* the body of problems.” The supplied verbal noun—explanation, acquisition or attainment—establishes the correct relation between the otherwise mismatched terms.

This corrective procedure must be performed for each of the thirty-five theoretical combinations rather than assuming that, once an abstract relation of inclusion has been proved possible, the author's wording is already stylistically appropriate. The point is the difference between **logical coherence of a proposed relation** and **idiomatic suitability of its linguistic expression**.
records.editorial: Q163 source sentence continues to the end of Q164 and closes before a NEW textual heading at Q165. The next printed page begins 'حواشي مقدمة علم المنطق' and RESTARTS local gloss numbering at (1); do not continue with a false note141 from that new section.
records.revision: Stage109 new source-linked preface H note; Qum digitally searchable text, not photographically collated

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله أي هذه مقدمة
records.english:
On the explanation “that is, this is an introduction”: the word *muqaddima* is a predicate of an omitted demonstrative subject, “this.” This follows the basic order that the subject is definite and the predicate indefinite. Others instead make “an introduction” the subject, with an omitted predicate: “an introduction [is concerned] with defining logic, explaining the need for it, and stating its subject.” An objection arises that a completely indefinite noun cannot ordinarily serve as the subject of a statement. Several replies are given. One can treat the indefiniteness as specially qualified by the tanwīn of magnification—signalling the many benefits of this introduction—or of diminution—signalling the brevity of its expressions. Alternatively place the omitted predicate before it: “In the definition of logic, the need for it, and its subject, there is an introduction,” like “In the house is a man.” A more general response judges the admissibility of an indefinite subject by whether the sentence conveys information, not by a fixed list of formal qualifications. Thus “A tree prostrated” and “A star fell just now” can inform the hearer, whereas a bare “A man is standing” may lack informative force in the relevant context.

A further objection targets the original analysis “this is an introduction.” Does the demonstrative not designate the three matters mentioned—the definition, need, and subject—whereas the introduction is not identical with those matters but is an exposition *about* them? Even granting this distinction, one need not take “this” to point to the three items themselves; it can point instead to the specifically arranged words and meanings that introduce them. The same response is available to those who understand the suppressed subject as “these matters.”
records.editorial: Entire p165 numbered note1 in first pass; the objection concerns reference and identity, not just definite-vs-indefinite forms.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, with separate reported ʿAbd al-Raḥīm comment
records.arabicLemma: قوله يتبين فيها أمور ثلاثة
records.english:
The words “three matters are explained in it” raise a problem about literal containment. The treatment is comparable to the prior discussion of “the first division is in logic”: a thing and what is contained in it must not be identical in precisely the same respect. One proposal, connected with al-Taftāzānī's commentary on the *Talkhīṣ*, distinguishes the *introduction to a science* from the *introduction to a book*. The former comprises what must be known in order to embark intelligently on the discipline—its definition, end and subject. The latter is the portion of a writer's discourse placed ahead of the principal subject because it is connected to and useful for that subject, whether or not the science strictly depends on it. The former could then be said to contain the latter, avoiding literal self-containment. Another proposal considers the three preliminary matters themselves as parts of the introduction, as one says that a particular inquiry occurs “in” a particular chapter.

A reported comment from ʿAbd al-Raḥīm challenges the supposition that “introduction to a book” is necessarily a new technical expression unsupported by usage. Writers regularly name their leading portions introductions, chapters, sections, *namṭ*, *tanbīh* or *ishāra*, and such designations cannot be confined to one prescribed vocabulary. The source compares an introduction with the advance detachment of an army, from which “what goes before” can be extended to a beginning. A further response by Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī distinguishes two aspects: the referent of “introduction” in the two analyses (science vs book), and whether containment applies separately to each of the three topics or to the topics taken collectively.
records.editorial: The whole p165–166 dossier combines signed prose by different voices; this note is an analytic first pass, NOT full literal transcription of each quote. Keep incomplete pending clause/signature collation.

records.speaker: Printed lemma with no independent authorial signature
records.arabicLemma: وهو آلة قانونية تعصم مراعاتها الذهن عن الخطأ في الفكر
records.english: “It is a rule-governed instrument whose observance protects the mind from error in thought.”
records.editorial: This numbered item reproduces a source lemma/definition. Its being one line does not require a longer explanatory paragraph.

records.speaker: Printed variant notation (خ ل)
records.arabicLemma: وجه ( خ ل )
records.english: “Way” or “aspect” (*wajh*): recorded as a variant reading (*nuskha ukhrā* / “in another copy”).
records.editorial: A reported alternative in the searchable print; NO independent manuscript witness is supplied or certified, so do not emend the principal text.

records.speaker: Printed lemma
records.arabicLemma: وهو التحرز عن وقوع الخطاء في الفكر
records.english: “It is to guard oneself against the occurrence of error in thinking.”
records.editorial: Short printed gloss/lemma; source's spelling of al-khaṭaʾ is not a verified independent manuscript variant.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, p.14 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: وموضوعه المعلومان التصوري والتصديقي
records.english: “Its subject is the two things already known: the conceptual and the assertoric, considered insofar as they lead respectively to two unknown things, one conceptual and one assertoric.”
records.editorial: al-Taqrīb's source-defined subject of logic, not a new proof of a formal object; note is a single quoted proposition.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.14, quoting al-Khaṭṭāʾī; separate ʿAbd al-Raḥīm and Muḥammad ʿAlī comments
records.arabicLemma: وهي مأخوذة من مقدمة الجيش
records.english:
On “it is derived from the vanguard of an army”: *muqaddima* is the group that proceeds before the rest of the army. Transferring the term to an introductory section of a book may be a new technical assignment, making it literally applicable in that convention, or a metaphor, like calling a brave man a lion. The likeness is that both are portions of a larger whole placed before the remainder.

Al-Khaṭṭāʾī suggests another possibility: the term was originally an adjective whose qualified noun was omitted, then used for a group of meanings or words which precedes the science or the rest of the book. The feminine ending may signal the transfer from adjectival to nominal use, or correspond to an implicitly feminine noun such as *ṭāʾifa* (“group”). Whether the resulting use is literal or figurative depends on whether the adjective is considered a general property of being advanced or a noun conventionally assigned to a specific kind of advance detachment.

The following, separately introduced ʿAbd al-Raḥīm passage compares the meanings of *muqaddima* with kasra or fatḥa on the dāl. The common pronunciation with kasra looks like an active participle; however the author's act of putting a section first might suggest a passive participle. A response takes the base verb in an intransitive sense, “to go forward,” making the preceding material properly active in advancing; another considers the active form as indicating that the section, by enabling insight, effectively puts itself forward. That answer faces an objection from the usual rule that the intensive causative form is transitive, though the rule may be predominant rather than without exceptions.
records.editorial: Substantial cross-page translation selection; the source includes multiple separately introduced voices and examples requiring full line-by-line collation, so remain partial.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: إشارة إلى أن المقدمة يطلق على معنيين آخرين
records.english: The commentator signals that *muqaddima* also has two other uses. First, it is a proposition made a component of a syllogism or other proof. Second, it is something on which the validity of an argument depends—for example, in the first syllogistic figure, the minor premise's being affirmative and the major premise's being universal. The second use is broader than the first, since it includes conditions of an inference as well as its constituent propositions.
records.editorial: The two logical senses of premise are distinct from the earlier book/science introduction distinction.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: والمراد منها هاهنا
records.english:
The words “what is intended by it here” specify that this occurrence means *the introduction to the book*, not the introduction to the science, as the term is used in some other works. The glossator has already distinguished them and directs the reader back to that discussion.

The definition of the present introduction as a “portion of discourse” is the definition of a book's introduction. That is why the author does not say that the science's problems necessarily depend on it, as one would when defining a science's introduction. The small word “here” is thus significant. Al-Sayyid al-Sharīf makes an analogous observation: in syllogistic reasoning the word “premise” means either a proposition entering the proof or something on which its soundness depends, including conditions such as affirmative minor, its actuality and universal major in the first figure.
records.editorial: Source note ends Q167 before numbered 10. Preserve al-Sharīf as a quoted authority.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, with separately cited al-Taqrīb
records.arabicLemma: إن كان الكتاب عبارة عن الألفاظ
records.english:
If “book” means its expressions, its “introduction” is a portion of the book's words placed before the principal discourse. If “book” refers to the meanings signified, the introduction may denote knowledge on which the science depends. The source criticizes proliferating word–meaning distinctions which obscure the genuine difference between the preliminary material necessary for a science and a literary introduction which assists comprehension without constituting that discipline.

The glossator rejects making the introduction to a science depend entirely on the author's act of ordering words. Some preliminary investigations, including the definition of a science, its subject and its need or purpose, are intellectual foundations of the discipline; introductory discussion of technical terminology can instead be indispensable merely to understanding a particular book's expressions. The long continuation is concerned with whether a philosophical introduction must itself be a constituent of the science and whether distinguishing the two introductions produces a useful explanation.
records.editorial: Long numbered note extends across Q167–168 and contains a separate source citation. Rendered as selected argument, not certified complete translation; remains PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (after al-Taqrīb citation)
records.arabicLemma: أي من الكلام اللفظي كما هو ظاهر
records.english:
This means “from verbal discourse,” as is clear from the context. A *ṭāʾifa* is a group or portion. Some authorities put its minimum at three or four, others at two or three. Its form is among adjectives that have come to be used substantively, as though the original expression were “a group which separates itself from something.”

It is reported from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās, however, that a *ṭāʾifa* may denote even one person or more. This accords with al-Jawharī's general explanation of it as a “piece of something.” Qurʾān 9:122, which speaks of a party going forth from every group to acquire religious understanding, is interpreted as allowing a single person, or a pair, to comprise the party. The plural pronoun in the following words does not require each individual *ṭāʾifa* to contain a plurality; it can refer to the multiple parties collectively conveyed by the context.
records.editorial: Lexical reports and Qurʾānic exegesis are the glossator's cited authorities, not independently authenticated interpretations.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يخفى أن ارتباط المقصود إنما هو بمعاني تلك الطائفة
records.english:
It is obvious that the principal topic is connected to the *meanings* conveyed by that group of expressions, not to the expressions considered merely as sounds or letters. Likewise, what is beneficial for the subject is the meanings, not the words simply as words. Hence one may supply an omitted genitive: “because the purpose is connected with *their meanings*, and *their meanings* are beneficial to it.”

Alternatively no omission is needed. Since expressions are the means through which knowledge is communicated and received, the connection and benefit are attributed to them figuratively.
