On the first analysis there is figurative omission (*majāz al-ḥadhf*), and on the second there is figurative attribution (*majāz fī al-isnād*).
records.editorial: Clearly distinguishes ellipsis from attribution to instruments of teaching.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.14 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وإن كان عبارة عن المعاني
records.english: “And if it [the book] consists of meanings”: in that case the introduction is an *introduction to the science* rather than to the book's verbal presentation.
records.editorial: Short quotation from al-Taqrīb; subject/reference from adjacent main commentary.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يعني الاحتمالات السبعة المذكورة للقسم الأول آنفا
records.english: That is, the seven possibilities for the referent of “the first division” which were mentioned earlier.
records.editorial: The seven choices distinguish words, meanings and inscriptions, singly or in their combinations; this item is a reference to previous discussion, not a full exposition.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.14–15 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وتجويز الاحتمالات الأخر في الكتاب
records.english:
The author says “An introduction concerning the definition of logic, the need for it and its subject.” Yet if the *introduction* is itself simply those three matters, how can one say the three matters are *in* it without making container and contained identical?

Any answer available for the earlier expression “the first division is in logic” is also available here, since the same problem arises. But the commentators do not rehearse all seven possible referents of a book's division and the five possible meanings of logic. Rather they say that “introduction” refers to expressions, while the three matters refer to meanings: the expressions serve to explain those meanings. The present critic asks why the many alternative repairs were enumerated for the previous case but not for this one, since the original motive for the enumeration has not disappeared.
records.editorial: Quoted critical question about inconsistent prolixity of the commentary; not endorsed as the sole proper resolution.

records.speaker: Short al-Taqrīb gloss
records.arabicLemma: أي جزء الكتاب
records.english: That is, a part of the book.
records.editorial: A one-line gloss specifying the referent; not a full prose treatise.

records.speaker: Short al-Taqrīb gloss
records.arabicLemma: أي لم يزيدوا من الكتاب والمقدمة إلا الألفاظ والمعاني
records.english: That is, in analysing the book and its introduction they considered nothing beyond expressions and meanings.
records.editorial: This identifies which of the earlier seven referent combinations were actually used.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī; later al-Karmī passage separately quoted
records.arabicLemma: قوله هو الصورة الحاصلة
records.english: On “knowledge is the form that comes to be [in the intellect]”: some define knowledge as the soul's reception of such a form, and others as the form of the object coming to be present in the intellect. On the first interpretation it is assigned to the category of quality; on the second, to that of passion or reception; on the third, as some analyse the cognitive relation, to the category of relation. This is not the place for a full decision among these philosophical accounts; the issue belongs in extended works of philosophy.
records.editorial: Short printed note18 closes at the source signature. A subsequent much later quotation from Shaykh Muḥammad al-Karmī criticises formal definitions of knowledge; keep it separately attributed and NOT as note18.

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Shaykh Muḥammad al-Karmī, a later separate quoted intervention (excerpt)
unnumberedFollowing.ar: أنا لم أجد تعريفا للعلم ... حقيقة العلم انكشاف الواقع
unnumberedFollowing.en: The later cited author criticizes the definitions of knowledge that reduce it to the mere occurrence of a form, favouring the disclosure of things as they actually are. A representation can seem to reflect reality while in fact deceiving the knower. Thus a good definition must distinguish truthful disclosure from imagined or illusory presentation. This is a selected translation of the quoted objection, NOT the whole modern insertion; its speaker/date must be registered separately from the earlier Arabic gloss.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, following separate quoted al-Taqrīb discussion
records.arabicLemma: قوله والمصنف لم يتعرض بتعريفه
records.english:
Why did Taftāzānī divide knowledge into conception and assent before defining knowledge itself? Division is a judgment about a thing; one might expect the thing to be understood before judgments are made about it. Three explanations are offered. First, a preliminary conception “in some respect” suffices for division: one need only recognise the familiar use of “knowledge” in the discipline. Grammarians similarly divide an exception into connected and disconnected kinds without first supplying an exhaustive definition of the exceptional term. Second, knowledge's definition is already familiar, so the author omits it for brevity. Third, the concept of knowledge is self-evident through experience, as al-Rāzī is reported to hold. Knowledge is among the qualities apprehended by introspection, like hunger, thirst and satiety.

A further argument appeals to ordinary speakers: even people untrained in logical definition, when asked “Do you know this?”, readily answer yes or no. They must therefore grasp the concept of knowledge well enough to understand the question. The glossator objects that neither introspection nor such answers proves that the *word* ʿilm has a self-evident lexical signification. One may immediately encounter an instance or grasp the general concept while still requiring an explanation that this word has been assigned to it.

An attempted defence distinguishes real definition from verbal explanation. The cited arguments might establish that one does not require a real definition of knowledge, while leaving lexical explanation open. The objection to the common-speaker argument also turns on whether the listener already knows the word's conventional assignment. If he does, he may answer without knowing the full real nature; if he does not, he cannot grasp the question merely by hearing it. The author later recognises that the arguments were perhaps directed only toward the impossibility or unnecessary character of a *real* definition, not a verbal gloss.

A further objection says knowledge cannot be defined at all: we know everything by knowledge, so knowing knowledge through something else would be circular. One answer is that knowing an object does not require explicit knowledge of the linguistic assignment of ʿilm. Another distinguishes the universal cognition which is supposedly to be defined from the particular cognitions through which we apprehend things; the supposed circle then equivocates on “knowledge.” The discussion ends by asking why Taftāzānī mentioned assent before conception, though conception is prior in nature as either a part or condition of assent: the answer invokes the greater dignity of assent's positive character compared with conception understood privatively.
records.editorial: Long source note extends Q169–170 with intertwined authorial objections and replies. This is a substantive selected first pass, not a claim of full clause-by-clause translation. Leave PARTIAL pending source/voice collation.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.15, critical anonymous voice
records.arabicLemma: قوله العلم إن كان إذعانا للنسبة فتصديق وإلا فتصور
records.english:
The author's words divide knowledge as follows: if it is an assent (*idhʿān*) to a relation, it is *taṣdīq*; otherwise it is *taṣawwur*. A critical commentator objects to allowing all other mental states into the latter category. He argues that genuine knowledge is disclosure of things as they are. When an affirmative or negative predicative relation between a subject and predicate is genuinely disclosed and the soul recognises and accepts that relation, the resulting act is assent. If the disclosure occurs without acceptance, the commentator describes a refusal or resistance, not an additional piece of genuine disclosed knowledge. When an isolated individual, scattered individuals, or an incomplete relation is made present—“Zayd,” “ʿAmr and Khālid,” “Zayd's servant”—we instead have conception, the presentation of their forms.

On this view it is a mistake to count performative or constructive sentences as conceptions of objective reality, since an *inshāʾ* brings about what is said rather than reporting an already existing predicative fact. The same critic rejects counting a complete assertoric relation entertained without assent—such as a fictional image, doubt or mere conjecture—as a true disclosure of reality merely because it is a mental presentation.

In his stronger formulation, assent is a condition or event of the soul, not a four-part compound of subject, predicate, relation and act of acceptance. The fact that these constituents can be described does not make the psychological act of assent simply their aggregate. The source polemically dismisses the compound theory; this is the critical writer's position rather than a claim that all historical logicians accepted it.
records.editorial: Long al-Taqrīb debate across Q170–171; chosen passages translated and argument mapped but not certified fully clause-by-clause. Author attribution and editorial insertion need control.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: فسر النسبة الحكمية بالنسبة التامة الخبرية
records.english:
The “judgmental relation” (*nisba ḥukmiyya*) is explained as the complete reportable relation, affirmative in an affirmative proposition and negative in a negative one. Some instead maintain that the relation must be an affirmative restrictive relation in either case, lest the negative judgment turn into an affirmative assertion concerning nonoccurrence.

That objection works only if a restrictive relation is itself made the explicit subject of a further judgment—for example, “the relation of nonestablishment between the terms does not obtain.” It does not apply when one simply conceives the complete predicative relation expressed in “Zayd is not a writer” and then assents to it.

The correct analysis, the writer contends, treats the judgmental relation as complete and reportable. Philosophers agree that conceiving a judgmental relation precedes the occurrence of judgment. The relation must therefore be conceivably complete before assent is added. One can conceive a subject, predicate and complete predicative link without assenting and later assent without having separately entertained an additional restrictive relation between them. Introspection supports this distinction.
records.editorial: Contrast between complete assertoric relation and restrictive relation is the focus; avoid treating the writer's claim of philosophical unanimity as verified consensus.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أنهم اختلفوا في حقيقة التصديق
records.english:
There are three views of the reality of *taṣdīq*. The philosophers say it is the very act of assent and judgment. Al-Rāzī and his followers treat it as a compound of four items: the conception of what is judged about (subject), of what is attributed (predicate), of the predicative relation between them, and assent. The author of *al-Kashf* and his followers treat it as the first three taken in the condition of judgment's accruing to them; this is known as the newer school.

Thus under the first view judgment is identical with assent; under the second it is one part of assent; under the third it is external to the three conceived elements and attaches to them as an accident. Taftāzānī selects the first when he writes “knowledge, if it is assent to a relation, is taṣdīq.” Further detail belongs in longer treatises, not this brief gloss.
records.editorial: Direct three-school map of taṣdīq: simple judgment; compound of four; three cognitions with judgment as accident.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (signature at Q173)
records.arabicLemma: قوله فقد اختار المصنف مذهب الحكماء
records.english:
The assertion that Taftāzānī chose the philosophers' position requires distinguishing two different questions. The first concerns the *nature of assent* (*taṣdīq*). For the philosophers it is the act of judgment, an intellectual apprehension accompanied by assent toward a complete predicative relation. It differs from simple conception in kind, not merely in having a different object. For al-Rāzī and his followers it is a compound of four constituents—conception of subject, predicate and relation, together with the act of judgment. Conceiving the three is a prerequisite of simple assent on the first theory; it is a *part* of assent on the second.

The distinction is relevant to logic's purpose. Conceived unknowns are acquired through an explanatory statement (*qawl shāriḥ*), whereas the act of assent is acquired through a proof (*ḥujja*). If assent is a simple intellectual act, these two kinds of acquired knowledge can be distinguished according to their acquisition. A composite containing several conceptual elements acquired in one way and an additional judgment acquired in another does not as naturally admit one distinctive procedure of acquisition.

Some attempt to reconcile the views by saying that the same assent is simple when considered as a whole and composite upon analysis into its presupposed contents. But al-Rāzī expressly calls assent the aggregate of conceptions and judgment, and contrasts composite with simple in *al-Mulakhkhaṣ*. Treating his stated composition as merely a different way of viewing a simple act obscures that explicit disagreement.

The second question concerns the *constituents of a proposition*. The older philosophers are described as counting three: subject, predicate and complete affirmative or negative predicative relation. Later philosophers count four by adding the obtaining or nonobtaining of the positive restrictive relation, motivated by cases of doubt. One can conceive a relation without judging whether it obtains; the cognition of obtaining/nonobtaining appears to be an additional element.

An opposing account replies that the same relation can be conceived without assent and apprehended with assent, without multiplying components. Some later writers distinguish the two considerations of the same relation—conceived and judged—and explain the different counts as analytic rather than numerical. The author of *Sharḥ al-Maṭāliʿ* is cited for allowing four elements upon detailed analysis. Taftāzānī's wording, however, describes assent to *the complete predicative relation*, and his later treatment of categorical propositions appears to require three formal parts. The source considers whether a suppressed “occurrence of” could be supplied to restore four parts, but rejects that as an interpretation contrary to his explicit later exposition.
records.editorial: Extensive Q171–173 numbered argument rendered as structured partial English; full Arabic and speaker boundaries still require clause-level audit. Do not mark complete.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الأولى أن يزيد عليه تصور النسبة الحكمية
records.english: It would have been better to add the conception of the predicative relation to the list. Al-Rāzī's position is that assent is compounded of *four* elements, not merely three, as already explained. Yet the commentator's goal here was not to investigate every constituent of al-Rāzī's position; it was to identify what distinguishes that view from the philosophers' account. The omission is therefore understandable.
records.editorial: Reports an editorial desideratum and its contextual excuse, not a change actually present in the matn.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله واختار مذهب القدماء
records.english:
The philosophers agree that assent itself is judgment and is not a compound containing the three prior conceptions. They disagree, however, about the composition of the *proposition*. The earlier philosophers count three constituents: the subject, the predicate, and the complete affirmative or negative assertoric relation. Later philosophers add a fourth: the occurrence or nonoccurrence of that relation.

Taftāzānī chooses the former position, since he makes the object of assent the predicative relation itself, rather than a distinct “occurrence” or “nonoccurrence” of the relation as the later account would.
records.editorial: Distinguishes *the act of assent* from *the logical proposition*; source note ends before no.26.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: بفتح اللام أي ما يتعلق به الإذعان
records.english: Read the word with fatḥa on its lām, denoting that to which assent is related—the object or correlate of assent. It can be incorrectly written or pronounced with kasra; the latter reading is plainly more remote in this context.
records.editorial: Reported pronunciation correction only; no independent manuscript witness.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: صفة للمتعلق لا للإذعان
records.english: The description qualifies what assent is *related to*, not the act of assent itself. Assent or judgment is not a constituent of the proposition; it is directed toward the proposition's final constituent, its predicative relation.
records.editorial: A grammatical attachment changes the claimed ontology of the proposition.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.16 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله والحكم الذي هو الجزء الأخير للقضية
records.english: The phrase should be understood as referring to the *object of judgment*, which is the proposition's last constituent—the predicative relation. A judgment concerning an affirmative or negative predicative relation is necessarily directed toward that relation.
records.editorial: Quoted correction in al-Taqrīb, not original principal commentator's note.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, followed by later separate al-Karmī quote
records.arabicLemma: قوله لا وقوع النسبة الثبوتية التقييدية
records.english: The restriction “occurrence or nonoccurrence of the positive restrictive relation” is awkward. It would be better to say “reportable relation” (*nisba khabariyya*) instead. Likewise, qualifying the predicative relation by “restrictive” adds no useful distinction on the reading assumed here, since, in the commentator's claim, the reportable relation already involves a restriction or predication.
records.editorial: A later separate comment by Shaykh Muḥammad al-Karmī on the different technical uses of 'restrictive' immediately follows and must not be counted as the numbered note29.

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Shaykh Muḥammad al-Karmī, separate later printed quotation after note29
unnumberedFollowing.en: The late commentator criticizes the phrase “a complete restrictive relation”: a complete assertoric connection already predicates something of a subject, whereas “restrictive relation” is more normally reserved for incomplete relational or adjectival constructions. He therefore regards the added qualification as misleading. This is a separately quoted critical gloss, not an independently verified variant of the historical principal commentary.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.15–16 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وقوع النسبة أو لا وقوعها
records.english:
What precisely is meant by the “occurrence or nonoccurrence of the relation”? If it means the affirmative or negative form actually uttered in a proposition, or entertained inwardly as a mental proposition, it is simply another way of describing an affirmative or negative relation. It adds no genuinely new constituent. If instead “occurrence” means the proposition's actual establishment in reality, and “nonoccurrence” its absence there, that is a different matter from the affirmative or negative form of speech or imagination. A spoken or mentally conceived affirmative can disagree with reality, just as an uttered negative can be false.

The commentator insists that the soul's proper assent is directed toward a relation disclosed as affirmative or negative by reality. An assent made without such real disclosure may be nothing more than acceptance of an illusion or misleading presentation. One should therefore not assume that the mere occurrence of a positive/negative verbal or imagined form makes a further fourth proposition-component.

If “occurrence” is construed as the existence of the relation in reality, that does not straightforwardly support treating it as an additional *part of a proposition* either. It may be a relation between proposition and extramental state of affairs rather than a further constituent of the internally structured proposition. On the critic's premises, the older/later philosophers' disagreement over three or four components is therefore partly sustained by shifting the meaning of “occurrence” between linguistic, mental and actual senses.
records.editorial: Long printed Q173–174 al-Taqrīb critique; full argumentative English synopsis but some Arabic distinctions omitted, so PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وسيشير المصنف
records.english:
The words “the author will indicate” forestall an objection. His description of judgment as assent to the relation alone does not, merely on its face, prove he accepts the earlier philosophers' three-part proposition. One might supply a suppressed genitive and coordination: “assent to the occurrence or nonoccurrence of the relation.” Such omissions are not unknown in eloquent Arabic. For example, Qurʾān 16:81 mentions garments guarding against heat, from which cold may also be understood, and Qurʾān 87:9 commands reminding if it benefits, with a disputed understanding of the unmentioned contrary case.

The reply is that the author later explicitly treats the proposition as having three constituents. It would then be illegitimate to impose the four-part interpretation on this earlier wording, since the hypothetical ellipsis would explain him in a way he does not accept. Changing his position or silently assuming he is merely reporting someone else's is implausible. The apparent wording also deserves interpretive priority unless a reason for an alternative reconstruction is established.
records.editorial: The Qurʾānic examples are alleged parallels for possible ellipsis; their exegetical strength is not established here.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.16 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: وسيُشير المصنف إلى تثليث أجزاء القضية
records.english: The promised indication occurs where the author says that if a categorical judgment attributes something to something else or denies it, the proposition is affirmative or negative; the judged-about is its subject (*mawḍūʿ*), what is attributed its predicate (*maḥmūl*), and what signifies the relation its copula (*rābiṭa*). He says nothing about “occurrence or nonoccurrence of the relation” as an additional fourth constituent, either expressly or by implication.
records.editorial: Quoted future-text concordance. Actual Taftāzānī matn should be checked as a separate T-family source.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي تقييدية إضافية
records.english: That is, a restrictive relation may be genitive or relational, like the preceding example; or adjectival, as in “a standing man”; or another incomplete construction, such as “the one whose father struck [someone].” Such relations are not identical with an independent complete report.
records.editorial: Clarifies technical *nisba taqyīdiyya* as an incomplete relation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أن من تصور النسبة الحكمية
records.english:
A person who conceives a predicative relation can have several distinct states. First, the conceived image may influence the soul, stirring attraction or repulsion, even when the intellect recognises that the opposite is true. Rhetorical phrases such as “wine is flowing ruby, delightful,” or “honey is bitter and nauseating,” produce this *takhyīl* (imaginative impression).

If it does not have that effect, and the two sides—being and nonbeing—appear evenly balanced with no preference, the state is *shakk* (doubt). If one side is preferred without certitude, the less likely side considered is *wahm* (conjecture) and the more likely side *ẓann* (opinion). Where there is definite judgment, the author distinguishes cases in which the negative side is fixed and those in which the positive side is asserted. He further distinguishes judgments corresponding to reality from those which do not; an entrenched false judgment is *jahl murakkab* (compound ignorance), whereas a judgment agreeing with reality is *yaqīn* (certainty) when immune to further doubt or *taqlīd* (unexamined acceptance) when susceptible to it.

The resulting classification is said to have eight forms. It is not acceptable to label every one as assent in the relevant technical sense. Imaginative impression, doubt, and mere weaker apprehension lack judgment; the glossator also sets apart the negative case as he has defined it. The remaining forms are treated as assent. Therefore “assent” in the original division must be taken broadly enough to embrace probable opinion (*ẓann*) rather than only the highest certitude (*yaqīn*). The proposed eightfold count is a local classification of mental states; its labels are not automatically equivalent to those of all other logic schools.
records.editorial: Source eightfold taxonomy; exact distribution of 'falsehood' vs 'compound ignorance' merits further clarification but sequence/conditions are rendered.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله بمعنى القسمة
records.english:
The clarification “in the sense of division” prevents a misunderstanding of the author's sentence. Because the form *iftiʿāl* is often intransitive, one might take *iqtisām* to mean “accepting division,” then insert an omitted preposition before “necessity and acquisition.” That would yield: conception and assent are divided by necessity and acquisition.

But, the glossator argues, al-Zamakhsharī's *Asās al-Balāgha* also uses *iqtisām* transitively in the sense of actively dividing. There is then no reason to supply the omitted preposition. Conception and assent *divide* necessity and acquisition. This does not mean conception is assigned wholly to one and assent wholly to the other—as though one person were allotting two different sorts of property to separate recipients. Rather, each of conception and assent receives a share in each of the two kinds. It resembles the way a noun is divided into definite and indefinite, declinable and indeclinable, explicit and pronominal, simple and construct forms.

On the intended reading, then, both conception and assent can be immediate and both can be acquired. The syntactic construction conveys the intended logical division, but not by taking the whole of necessity as conception and the whole of acquisition as assent, or conversely.
records.editorial: Transitivity of *iqtisām* used to preserve both taṣawwur and taṣdīq under both necessary and acquired cognition.

records.speaker: Shaykh Muḥammad al-Karmī (modern quoted insertion)
records.arabicLemma: ونجد كثيرا من أفعال باب الافتعال متعدية بأنفسها
records.english: Many verbs belonging to the pattern *iftiʿāl* govern their objects directly: for example, verbs meaning “carry it,” “take it back,” “cut it out,” or “pluck it.” Their direct transitivity need not be explained artificially by positing that they incorporate the meanings of other transitive verbs. The author regards that manoeuvre as an arbitrary complication.
records.editorial: Explicitly MODERN printed attribution to al-Karmī. Count as a printed numbered item but never as sixteenth-century al-Yazdī or early glossator speech.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: هو ما يكتسب بلا نظر والكسبى ما يكتسب بالنظر
records.english: The immediate or necessary is what is obtained without discursive inquiry (*naẓar*); the acquired or theoretical is what is obtained through inquiry. This formulation differs from the familiar definitions: necessary knowledge is what does not *depend* on inquiry, and theoretical knowledge what does depend on it. The distinction matters for knowledge that is ordinarily acquired discursively but might also be attained in a sudden intuition (*ḥads*) or by a specially endowed intellect. On the dependence formulation, that particular occurrence would cease to be theoretical and the definitions would fail either to include all the intended cases or to exclude the others. Describing how knowledge actually occurs—without or through inquiry—avoids the immediate ambiguity.
records.editorial: A conceptual objection about *dependency* vs *mode of acquisition*, not an independent proof of a metaphysical 'sacred soul'.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: يعني أن معنى كلام المصنف ظاهر
records.english:
The surface wording could seem to mean that conception and assent divide necessity and acquisition, making the first pair the *dividers* and the second pair what is *divided*. The principal purpose, however, is to show that each of conception and assent is divisible into immediate and acquired kinds. This can be understood implicitly in the stated division. If both conception and assent each take shares from the two classes, each must have an immediate kind and an acquired kind, just as a noun divides into definite/indefinite or other opposing grammatical classifications.

The main assertion is thus conveyed by implication (*iltizām*) and by indirect expression (*kināya*), rather than explicitly saying that conception and assent are each of two kinds. The commentator calls an indirect expression better and more eloquent than a bare statement because the conclusion is approached through something entailing it: in favourable cases, the existence of a necessary concomitant provides evidence for the intended meaning. One must nevertheless preserve the difference between an implication that actually follows and a rhetorical interpretation merely alleged to follow.
records.editorial: The note crosses Q175–176; this is its first-pass full argumentative summary, not independently scanned.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ضمنا وكناية
records.english:
Two explanations of *kināya* were already contrasted in the book's preface: al-Sakkākī and his followers define it as mentioning what necessarily accompanies something while intending the thing accompanied, with the literal meaning still potentially intended; another group reverses that relation. The present construction can support either explanation, because the two relevant divisions entail one another when the terms are understood correctly.

The glossator criticizes an interpretation which reduces the matter to simply reversing the order of a sentence, as in the proverbial “I presented the she-camel to the pool” instead of “I presented the pool to the she-camel.” Reversal is not in principle incompatible with indirect expression; one can use a reversal *and* speak by kināya. The critic might have intended indirect expression effected by a reversal, but that is not the same as defining kināya as reversal itself.
records.editorial: A distinction between structural inversion and indirect predication; explicitly preserves possibility of both.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وهي أبلغ وأحسن من التصريح
records.english:
Why is an indirect expression said to be more eloquent and beautiful than explicit speech? One answer likens it to establishing a claim by evidence. From the existence of the thing accompanied (*malzūm*) one may infer its necessary concomitant (*lāzim*), because the one cannot exist without the other. That explanation works readily for the account of kināya in which the thing accompanied is mentioned and the concomitant intended.

For al-Sakkākī's direction of inference—from the concomitant to the thing it accompanies—the explanation is less straightforward. A concomitant may be more general than the thing for which it is a concomitant, and the existence of what is general does not prove a specific instance. The argument can be repaired if the concomitant and its referent are coextensive or otherwise mutually entailing. Al-Sakkākī is cited as recognising the dependence of the inference on that equality. The full theory of rhetorical evidence would require more discussion than this note permits.
records.editorial: A rigorous scope qualification: a necessary consequence need not be convertible unless coextensive.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.16–17 (lexical gloss)
records.arabicLemma: جشم يجشم ... جشامة الأمر
records.english: The verb *jashima* means to undertake something with exertion or hardship. In the causative form *jashshamahu* or *ajshamahu*, it means to impose that burdensome task upon another person. This explains the earlier phrase about the effort required to construct a proof.
records.editorial: Short lexical item; no historical speaker identity beyond quoted al-Taqrīb heading.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله كما ارتكبه القوم
records.english:
The usual proof that some conceptions and assents are immediate and others theoretical argues by excluding two extremes. They cannot **all** be immediate, because in fact some objects of conception and some matters of judgment require deliberate inquiry. Nor can they **all** be theoretical, because if every cognition required a prior cognition, the acquisition of knowledge would be trapped in circular dependence or endless regress.

If a cognition A requires B, B requires C and C in turn requires A, the supposed acquisition of A would require A itself to precede its own acquisition—an impossibility. The infinite regress also seems to demand a completion of infinitely many prerequisites before the present cognition can occur. The glossator develops the distinctions between circularity and regress and the assumptions behind the impossibility of each.

An objection raises a possible eternal history of intellect: an infinite series of preparatory cognitions might be spread over an infinitely long past, with each preparing the next rather than being jointly present at one time. A response says this is unavailable on the theological premises which reject the eternity of souls and the world; the argument is therefore conditional upon those disputed premises and does not by itself prove that every kind of infinite causal sequence is impossible.

A final logical caution is important. The two types of cognition may not be absolutely isolated. If a conception could be acquired by an earlier assent or an assent by an earlier conception, the claim that **every conception** is theoretical might terminate in a necessary assent, and the claim that **every assent** is theoretical might terminate in a necessary conception. The standard proof therefore requires an additional premise restricting the cross-type acquisition routes. Without it, the proposed dilemma does not independently establish the twofold division *within each type*.
records.editorial: Extensive source Q176→177 with multiple objections and philosophical premises. Significant English analytic translation, but not fully clause-paired; remains PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.17 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وذلك أي ودليل بداهتها
records.english:
The point is to establish that immediate cognitions really occur. Reality is often disclosed to us spontaneously through ordinary dealings with the world. We encounter heat without seeking to know it, conceive what heat is, and learn of fire; we then judge that fire is hot, without having first constructed a deliberate proof. Thus a conception and a judgment can arise without paid effort or systematic inquiry. Thousands of similar everyday examples are available.

Theoretical cognition is equally evident: the very need for canons of inference and methods of evaluating proofs is to acquire and establish conclusions that do not simply arrive of themselves.
records.editorial: An appeal to spontaneous experience, not an independently established formal classification of particular sensings.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله كتصور الحرارة والبرودة
records.english:
By the conception of heat and cold is meant the intellect's grasp of the *universal concept*, acquired by means of particular sensations of heat and cold, not those particular sensations themselves. Heat itself can be present in the bodily organ which bears the power of touch. Its being present in that physical way is not, on this commentator's theory, knowledge, since knowledge is the form received in the intellect from the object.

There is no inconsistency between calling these concepts immediate and later giving the properties or characteristics of heat and cold in a scientific discussion. The latter treatment explains their attributes and judgments concerning them, rather than supplying for the first time the elementary apprehension needed to think of them.
records.editorial: Historical distinction between the causal occasion in sensation and the universal concept abstracted by intellect.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الملك جسم نوراني علوي
records.english:
The note describes an angel, in the inherited cosmological account, as a luminous upper-world body capable of taking different forms except those of a dog and pig; a jinn is described as a fiery lower-world body capable even of those forms. The spirit, by contrast, is described as an immaterial substance connected to the body as rose-water is connected to a rose.

These are quoted definitions within a premodern theological/cosmological vocabulary, not empirical anatomical propositions or universally agreed metaphysical definitions.
records.editorial: Short source crosses Q177–178; its cosmological assertions are faithfully attributed without modern factual endorsement.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أن ضرورية التصديق ونظريته عند الحكماء
records.english:
For the philosophers, assent is necessary or theoretical with respect to the act of judgment alone; they do not include the prior conceptions of the two terms and their relation in this classification. For al-Rāzī, by contrast, assent is a compound of four elements. Its being necessary therefore requires all four to be necessary; it is theoretical if at least one of its components is theoretical, even when the others are not. The same consequence holds for the followers of the view associated with the author of *al-Kashf*.

The extension of “necessary assent” is accordingly broader on the philosophers' simple-act account than on the composite accounts, while “theoretical assent” is broader on the composite accounts. A change in what counts as the *thing classified* changes the extension of its necessary and theoretical species.
records.editorial: Formal inclusion claim derives from different definitions of assent; source does not count all species as identical.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.17 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: هو ملاحظة المعقول لتحصيل المجهول
records.english:
The definition of inquiry (*naẓar*) as “considering an intelligible to obtain an unknown” would, the critic argues, be clearer if it said “considering something known to obtain something unknown.” The latter immediately conveys the thought that an item already disclosed is used to discover something concealed. The phrase “the intelligible” instead suggests what has already been apprehended by the rational faculty, without making the inferential transition as transparent.

The principal commentator gives several reasons for choosing “intelligible.” First, “knowledge” (*ʿilm*) is used in multiple senses, such as a form in the intellect, assent and certainty, and equivocal language in a definition is undesirable. The critic regards the list as verbal proliferation: knowledge properly refers to the disclosure of reality. Second, reasoning proceeds in intelligibles, especially universals, not bare particulars; an isolated particular is too determined to serve as a universal mediating term by which another is inferred. Third, the term maintains balanced rhyme with “the unknown.”

The critic suspects that the third reason was the chief motive. He adds that a particular is neither a suitable general means of acquiring a distinct particular nor usually something acquired by using another particular as a middle, because the individuating conditions separate them. The argument concerns the logical role of middle terms, not the claim that particular events can never be known by signs in ordinary life.
records.editorial: Rendered substance of the quoted al-Taqrīb note; traditional inference distinction is source-attributed.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي بطريق القصد كما هو المتبادر
records.english: “Through inquiry” should mean through an act of deliberate intention, as the wording and final purpose suggest. The definition is therefore not refuted by a case of sudden intuition (*ḥads*), in which the arranged premises arise all at once; in such an event the apprehension is not brought about by a deliberately chosen discursive procedure, but occurs without that voluntary direction.
records.editorial: Intention distinguishes formal inquiry from sudden intuition; no independent psychometric claim.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله نحو الأمر المعقول
records.english: The intelligible under consideration may be a conception or an assent; and the assent may be certain, probable or even mistaken in the specified sense. The expression is broad enough to include one known item or several, since a definition may employ a single term or a composite explanation. The definite article is therefore generic, indicating the class rather than a single preselected item.
records.editorial: Short scope clarification; note50 starts on Q178 but continues beyond, left for next stage.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله لتحصيل أمر غير معلوم
records.english:
The unknown sought through reflection may be either conceptual or assertoric. To discover the meaning of “human,” one may arrange the previously understood concepts “animal” and “rational”; to establish that the world is originated, one may assemble “the world changes” and “whatever changes is originated.” The starting elements must already be known in the relevant respect. Yet the result cannot already be known in precisely the respect in which it is sought, since that would be obtaining what one already possesses. It must be identified under another description so that inquiry can be directed toward it.

The note recalls al-Rāzī’s dilemma: if the object is known, inquiry is redundant; if utterly unknown, one cannot seek it. Knowing it in one respect and not in another appears to answer this dilemma, but the glossator reports a further objection: the known aspect cannot be sought as unknown, while the unknown aspect is not yet available to intention. A fuller dispute involving Sharaf al-Dīn al-Marāghī is expressly set aside by the source.
records.editorial: The closing Arabic explicitly declines to treat al-Marāghī’s objection in detail. This is a substantial partial translation, not an invented completion of that debate.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفي العدول عن لفظ المعلوم
records.english: The statement about departing from the word “known” supplies an answer to the objection that the author did not define inquiry as considering the known to obtain the unknown, even though knowledge and ignorance are the natural opposites.
records.editorial: Short printed gloss; the proposed alternative is attributed to the objector.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله منها التحرز عن استعمال اللفظ المشترك
records.english: “Knowledge” has several technical uses. It may signify a form present in intellect, encompassing conception and assent; it may also mean firm, unshakable, reality-conforming conviction, or belief in a broad sense including opinion, compound ignorance and imitation. A definition using such a shared expression without an indicator risks being read in the wrong sense. That is the reason advanced for choosing “intelligible” instead of “known.”
records.editorial: The list reports distinct inherited usages; it does not make compound ignorance genuine knowledge in every technical vocabulary.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أما الأول فلأن الجزئي إما أن يكون محسوسا
records.english: A particular can be apprehended through the five outward senses or through the inward powers traditionally enumerated as common sense, imagination, estimation, the compositive power and memory. Simply arranging several particular sensations does not produce another particular sensation or a universal as a logical inference. Nor does joining universals as such yield a determinate individual. On this account particulars are neither logical premises acquiring another particular nor conclusions acquired as particulars. “Intelligible” therefore points toward universals, whereas “known” can cover both particular and universal objects.
records.editorial: A historical restriction on *formal inferential acquisition*, not a denial of ordinary knowledge of particulars through signs.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: في بعض النسخ كتب هذه الحاشية قبل حاشية قوله وقد يقع فيه الخطاء
records.english: Some copies place this marginal note before the comment on “error may occur in it.” If that order was not a copyist’s inadvertence, it may have been chosen to bring the remarks on the subject of logic directly beside the gloss beginning “and its subject ...,” preserving the flow of the explanation. Another suggested motive is the beginner’s desire to learn the general rule as soon as possible. These are hypotheses about order, not independently collated readings of identified manuscripts.
records.editorial: Reported copy-order difference only; neither source copy nor reading has been authenticated.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: وقيل رومي موضوع في الأصل
records.english: One account says the word *qānūn* was originally a Greek or Roman expression for the ruling instrument used to draw writing lines, or more generally a writing ruler or grid. The *Qāmūs* defines it as the measure of anything; its plural is *qawānīn*.
records.editorial: Lexical attribution is reported, not independent etymological confirmation.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed pp.17–18 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله لمسطر الكتابة
records.english: A writing ruler straightens lines on a page. In technical usage a *qānūn* is a universal proposition from which the rules for many particular instances of its subject can be learned. For example, the grammatical rule “Every agent is nominative” applies to the agent in “Zayd stood,” “ʿAmr sat,” and indefinitely many other sentences.
records.editorial: Short quoted al-Taqrīb note; grammatical rule and its applications are examples, not a claim that every rule of logic concerns Arabic grammar.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفي الاصطلاح قضية كلية
records.english: The literal writing ruler and the technical universal rule are appropriately related: each is one thing by means of which many distinct results are attained. The technical use may be a settled conventional signification or an explicit metaphor; the former is preferred here.
records.editorial: Competing theories of technical lexical usage remain distinct.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله تعرف منها أحكام جزئيات موضوعها
records.english:
Apply the universal proposition as the major premise of an easily available minor premise. In “Zayd struck,” identify Zayd as the agent; combine “Zayd is an agent” with “Every agent is nominative,” and infer “Zayd is nominative.” The rule makes particular applications potentially available in advance; supplying the minor premise brings each to explicit actuality.

But the applications need not all be theoretical or unknown. Some are immediate, such as the familiar productivity of the first syllogistic figure. A rule still has the *capacity* to yield them, even if an individual conclusion is already self-evident. The description “judgments are learned from it” should accordingly be read in terms of suitability to support such judgments, not as asserting that every application actually requires learning.
records.editorial: Long source has reported variant «يتعرف بها»; it is not an independently certified manuscript reading. First-pass argument rendered, but source-line collation remains incomplete.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي قضية كلية إطلاقا لاسم الجزء
records.english: This means a universal proposition. The term for the decisive part is applied to the whole, just as “neck” can stand for a person or “eye” for a watcher. The part in question is central to the whole’s existence and use.
records.editorial: Brief metonymic explanation, not a new universal law.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وقد ينتهي إلى نقيضها
records.english: “It may end in its contradictory” is taken broadly: the outcome may be opposed to the earlier result by affirmation and negation, privation and possession, real contrariety, correlatives or a related form of incompatibility. The author illustrates error in the thoughts that generate assents because it is more conspicuous there. Error can also occur in the formation of conceptions, as disagreements about essential and descriptive definitions show. The omitted parallel example can therefore be understood by analogy.
records.editorial: Note begins p180, closes on p181 before (61); distinguish strict contradiction from the broader listed oppositions.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: القدم كعنب ضد الحدوث
records.english: *Qidam* is opposed to origination. The word *ʿālam* is treated in one account as a collective with no singular from its own form. It can signify a group of rational creatures, the totality of created things, the classes of angels and the two responsible kinds, or what reveals the Creator through substances and accidents. Different proposed etymologies derive it from a sign (*ʿalāma*) or knowledge (*ʿilm*).
records.editorial: Several lexicographical interpretations are juxtaposed; no single proposed etymology is certified.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ولا يخفى أن هذا أعم من أن يكون أحد الفكرين ناشئا من شخص
records.english: Contradictory results of reasoning can belong to different persons, since thinkers disagree; but they can also arise within one person's intellectual history, as the same inquirer changes judgments at different times. Even established scholars can adopt new positions. The case is not confined to public disputes between two writers.
records.editorial: Distinguishes disagreement across persons from a change in the same person over time.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وإلا لزم اجتماع النقيضين
records.english: When a person directly recalls having reasoned to one conclusion and then to its opposite, the conflict of the judgments is accessible by introspection. In disputes between different people, words alone do not guarantee that their internal beliefs contradict: a speaker may utter a position for display or some other reason. Error also affects conception, as shown by disagreement about *ḥadd* and *rasm*. The author's emphasis on assent may rest on its greater obviousness or on leaving the parallel conceptual case to analogy.
records.editorial: A distinction between contradictory utterances and actual opposed assents; it does not make all self-reports infallible.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله فلا بد من قاعدة كلية
records.english:
What is sought in practice is a judgment about a particular act of reasoning: is this inference sound or defective? Since no finite teacher can enumerate all future cases, the discipline supplies universal rules which can be applied when a case arises. A possible objection is that someone might gain insight without discursive reasoning, through purification of attention or intellectual disclosure. The reply restricts the claim to the *discursive reasoner qua reasoner*: logic is needed for monitoring such reasoning, not asserted to be the only possible route to every form of knowledge.

Another objection says that one might already know by immediate rational awareness which inferential methods are correct, and errors arise merely through inattentiveness. The reply invokes the occurrence of errors by sincere inquirers who aim at truth. In the context of using acquired inferential methods, unaided common sense does not always suffice to distinguish the sound from the defective.
records.editorial: Two-page note with further wording requiring a literal Arabic clause audit; source's restricted necessity of logic is preserved.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الناس في الأصل أناس حذفت همزته تخفيفا
records.english: The word *al-nās* has been explained as originally *unās*, with its hamza suppressed for ease, especially with the definite article. Another account calls it a collective lacking a singular of the same form and associates it with movement (*naws*). A cited lexicon allows a broader meaning covering jinn and humans, but in this passage the human community is intended.
records.editorial: Reports alternative lexical derivations; no single one independently established.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله بثلاث مقدمات
records.english: Why begin the proof that logic is needed by dividing cognition into conception and assent? Would it not suffice to distinguish knowledge acquired by reflection from that which arises without reflection? The answer is that the author wants to establish the need for logic in both its parts: the way leading to unknown conceptions and the way leading to unknown judgments. A genus can have two kinds without each species itself exhibiting both kinds. Without the more detailed initial divisions, one could suppose all conception immediate while only assent required acquisition, or conversely. The desired twofold need would not follow.
records.editorial: The note later queries whether the final premise proves need for logic itself or need to learn it; its logic is a distinction of conclusions.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله فهذه المقدمات الثلاث
records.english: The argument has three premises in its outward presentation but arguably four in substance, because the second combines two propositions: conception and assent each divide into immediate and acquired kinds, and theoretical knowledge is obtained from immediate knowledge.
records.editorial: A structural unpacking of the argument, not a new manuscript reading.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله فهذه المقدمات الثلاث تفيد احتياج الناس
records.english:
A familiar counterargument says that logic itself must be acquired, since otherwise its rules would be immediately evident and there would be no need to study it. But if every acquisition needs a previously acquired logical rule, the acquisition of logic would require another logic, producing a circle or regress. The proposed answer distinguishes the parts: some elementary logical rules are immediate, illustrated by the first syllogistic figure, while others are demonstrable from those basics, as the other figures are derived from the first. Logic is not entirely immediate and not entirely theoretical.

A different formulation alleges that logic *must* be immediately known to avoid the regress. Even if granted, that would show only that learning it is unnecessary, not that reasoning can dispense with it. A knower may rely on an already possessed logical principle when reaching further conclusions. The source warns that this dispute is difficult and sensitive to the distinction between possessing a norm, acquiring it and using it.
records.editorial: Long note p182→183 with two forms of objection, dialectical replies and internal nuance. This is an English analytical rendering, NOT full clause-by-clause source translation.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وعلم من هذا تعريف المنطق
records.english: The need for logic reveals its objective: to protect the inquirer in the activity for which the discipline is needed. Explaining that objective gives a descriptive account (*rasm*) of the science through its end. An objection says that a proper identifying characteristic must be coextensive with what it describes, whereas the same end might belong to many disciplines. The reply specifies the intended coextensive end rather than a purpose shared indiscriminately.
records.editorial: Purpose/definition argument should not be confused with an essential *ḥadd*.

records.speaker: al-Shamsiyya (quoted marginal dictum)
records.arabicLemma: وإنما قال تعصم مراعاتها ولم يقل نفسها
records.english: The author rightly says that *observing* logical rules protects thought, not that the mere possession of logic does. Trained logicians sometimes err because they fail to use the instrument.
records.editorial: Quoted short source under Shamsiyya; does not ascribe psychological infallibility to practitioners.

records.speaker: Mixed printed note and quoted al-Taqrīb, pp.18–19
records.arabicLemma: قوله فهاهنا ... وموضوعه المعلوم التصوري والتصديقي
records.english:
The original introduction promised three matters: the need for logic, its definition, and its subject. The first two have been addressed; the third identifies known conceptions and known assents *insofar as they can lead to unknown conceptions and assents*. This qualification excludes merely considering a known item without its ability to advance inquiry.

A later quoted critic accepts that a particular conceived object, qua particular, may not serve as an inferential middle. But he challenges the claim that some known propositions, such as “Fire is hot,” are incapable of leading to further conclusions. Combined with a general rule about the effects of heat, that statement can yield a result about fire. Its being obvious is irrelevant to whether it can function as a premise. The distinction should be between *capacity to lead* and actual profundity, not between respectable theoretical propositions and ordinary judgments.
records.editorial: The Q183→184 passage has a separate extended al-Taqrīb criticism; abbreviated, not complete translation. Preserve separate source voice.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله موضوع العلم
records.english: The commentator first defines the subject of a science generally, then applies the definition to logic. This provides a universal principle for the particular case: the items whose intrinsic attributes are investigated in logic are the known conceptual and assertoric objects; whatever has its intrinsic attributes investigated in a science is that science's subject; therefore these objects constitute logic's subject.
records.editorial: Explicit reconstructed inference is the glossator's application of the general subject formula.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, p.19, with separately introduced Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī discussion
records.arabicLemma: قوله موضوع العلم ما يبحث فيه عن العوارض الذاتية
records.english:
An intrinsic accident belongs to a subject through its own nature, or through something not foreign to that subject in the relevant explanatory sense; a foreign accident depends on an extraneous intermediary. Examples include wonder in human beings, occupying space through being a body, speech through rationality, and laughter associated with wonder. The source develops a list differentiated by whether the mediating factor is a constituent, equal in extension, more general, more specific or wholly separate. Cases mediated by something narrower or external are more readily classified as foreign; those mediated through a constituent or coextensive feature are disputed.

A separately introduced longer marginal intervention then compares older and later classifications. It reports agreement on three intrinsic and three foreign cases, with the case mediated by a more general constituent disputed; it also argues that the science should investigate its subject's intrinsic accidents because these genuinely describe that subject rather than another subject to which the property belongs more immediately.
records.editorial: Long Q184→185 technical register, NOT full line-by-line bilingual collation; modern/earlier speakers explicitly distinct. Follow-up source should preserve seven- or eightfold enumerations exactly.

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, independently introduced extended gloss after no.73
unnumberedFollowing.ar: اعلم : ان العوارض قسمان : اعراض ذاتية واعراض عرضية
unnumberedFollowing.en: A separate intervention distinguishes intrinsic and extrinsic attributes by the type and extension of the intermediary: the essence, an equal or more general constituent, or an external equal, broader, narrower or disjoint intermediary. The traditional classificatory dispute specifically concerns attributes through a more general internal constituent. It argues that each science studies the genuine properties of its own subject. This is an editorial synopsis of an unnumbered continuation, not a complete Arabic translation.
unnumberedFollowing.translationScope: editorial synopsis of separate historical speech

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الضمير المجرور في قوله فيه يعود إلى العلم
records.english: The pronoun in “in it” refers to the science, whereas “its accidents” refers to the entity identified as its subject. The subject of medicine is the human body in respect of health and disease; that of jurisprudence is the acts of responsible persons in respect of legal permissibility, prohibition, validity and invalidity; that of grammar is the word and utterance in respect of inflection and construction.
records.editorial: Examples explain the grammatical referents of the definition; not every discipline is thereby reduced to one undifferentiated subject.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي يرجع فيه إليها وذلك إما بجعل موضوع العلم موضوع المسألة
records.english: A particular question in a science may take the science's general subject as its own subject, or one of its kinds. Thus natural philosophy may investigate bodies as such or a kind of body; the scientific question may also establish an attribute connected through a broader consideration provided that the inquiry does not exceed the proper scope of the science. Comparable examples are drawn from jurisprudential judgments about intoxicants and natural philosophy's account of intermediate rest between two rectilinear motions. The argument answers a worry that some properties considered by sciences depend on narrower conditions and therefore would not qualify as intrinsic accidents of the general subject.
records.editorial: Long note crosses Q185→186, source distinction between subject and species of subject needs full clause-level check; keep partial.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أراد بالأمر ما يعم الداخل والخارج
records.english: “Intermediary” includes both internal and external factors. When it is required to be equal in extension to the subject, only two relevant cases remain: an equal internal constituent and an equal external property. Explaining the equal intermediary as necessarily external would therefore be too narrow.
records.editorial: Six-category partition reduced by equality condition; source examples include speech arising through rationality.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله كالضحك الذي يعرض
records.english:
The example of laughter arising through astonishment is intended in terms of a capacity or potentiality. Otherwise, if astonishment means an actual episode, it is narrower than humanity since humans are not always astonished; if it means only a capacity, an actual act of laughing may require more than that capacity. Taking both laughter and astonishment in the relevant potential sense is proposed as the repair.

A further question asks whether “one who is astonished” names an intelligible notion distinct from the individual, or the individual himself. On the first reading one risks assigning laughter first to the individual rather than to the abstract notion; on the second the intermediary becomes identical with the bearer rather than a genuinely explanatory middle. The source records this difficulty without decisively resolving it.
records.editorial: Substantive translation of both principal objections; note ends with an expressed invitation to reconsider.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يحتمل أن يكون إشارة إلى كل من الأبحاث المذكورة
records.english: The reference may point to any one of the preceding discussions, or to all of them. It may instead indicate that the figurative usage concerns the attribution of a property rather than a metaphor in a word or a grammatical inflection.
records.editorial: Uncertain referent explicitly preserved.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي عن عوارضه وهكذا الحال في قوله بل يبحث عن المعرف والحجة
records.english: The intended words are “about its accidents.” The same implicit qualification applies to “the science investigates the definition and the argument”: it investigates their properties rather than simply reproducing the defined subject itself.
records.editorial: Short contextual ellipsis clarification.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يقال إن البحث عن المعرف والحجة من هذه الحيثية
records.english: An objection says that investigating definition and proof *insofar as they lead to the unknown* is just investigating the leading itself; but if being a vehicle of discovery already forms part of logic's subject, the subject and its constituents cannot be investigated as though they were properties of themselves. The reply distinguishes **the fact or capacity of leading to an unknown**—the qualification defining the subject—from **the manner in which the leading occurs**, which is an attribute open to investigation. This avoids an identical subject/property claim.
records.editorial: Two distinct respects—leading as subject condition and manner of leading as investigated attribute.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فيكون من باب تسمية الدال باسم المدلول
records.english: Expressions such as “rational animal” are called definitions, and symbolic premise sequences are called syllogisms, but strictly it is their *meanings* that explain a nature or establish an inference. The words communicate those meanings and may receive their names by association. Logic's primary subject is therefore the intelligible contents of definitions and arguments, not sounds or written signs considered independently.
records.editorial: Do not infer that attention to logical language is irrelevant; it is instrumental to understanding the content.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله من قبيل تسمية السبب
records.english: A proof can be called a *ḥujja* because it causes victory in argument. This names the cause by the name of its result, as when rain is called “vegetation” because it brings vegetation about. The analogy explains the conventional transfer, not the literal identity of proof and victory.
records.editorial: The section ends on printed p187; p188 begins a different titled local-note series on signification.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb, printed p.20 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: حواشي التصورات بحث الدلالات قوله دلالة اللفظ
records.english:
Logic is primarily concerned with known concepts and judgments as means of acquiring further concepts and judgments. That purpose does not itself require studying the sounds of words. Nevertheless, traditional logic textbooks begin by discussing simple and compound expressions, univocal and gradated terms, and related distinctions because they assist the presentation of conceptual inquiry.

Signification in general occurs when cognition of one thing leads to cognition of another. Conventional verbal signification depends on the designation of an expression for a meaning; a sound never conventionally assigned to a meaning does not possess that particular signification. Within verbal conventional signification, *muṭābaqa* indicates the whole meaning assigned, *taḍammun* indicates a constituent part, and *iltizām* indicates an accompanying implication outside the meaning itself.
records.editorial: Long source note abbreviated, not a full literal English translation. The al-Taqrīb author should not be conflated with Yazdī.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: وذلك لأن ما يبين ويعرف ماهية الإنسان هو معنى الحيوان الناطق
records.english: What defines a human as a rational animal is the *meaning* of that expression, not merely the pronunciation. Otherwise someone ignorant of the language's word assignments would grasp the definition simply on hearing the words. Similarly, what demonstrates the world's origination is the understood content of the premises “the world changes” and “whatever changes is originated,” not their sounds.
records.editorial: Conceptual content versus linguistic vehicle.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: المراد من الحد هو التعريف الجامع المانع
records.english: The intended *ḥadd* here is a definition which includes all and only the things being defined.
records.editorial: A short definitional lemma.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي المباحث المذكورة في كتب الفن لا جميعها
records.english: The intended matters are those actually discussed in books of this discipline, not absolutely every possible inquiry. The following expression about explaining the conventional meanings of technical terms makes the restriction clear.
records.editorial: Scope restriction to textual teaching, rather than all sciences.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي مقدمة الفن لا جميع العلوم
records.english: The intended reference is to the introduction of this particular art, not to all sciences.
records.editorial: Single-sentence historical note.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الدلالة الالتزامية مهجورة في الحدود التامة
records.english: Logic needs an account of signification because technical rules concerning definitions distinguish whole, partial and implicative meanings. In a complete essential definition, an external implication cannot replace the defining content; the use of constituent meanings likewise has restrictions. The five predicables belong to the study of simple meanings, requiring a prior distinction between simple and compound expressions. Figurative and equivocal expressions are normally avoided in definitions unless a clarifying indicator is present. Univocal and gradated terms also matter: some allow a gradated expression to function as a genus while others deny it. These controversies explain the conventional introductory study of language.
records.editorial: First-pass paraphrase of the note's instructional dependency chain, not certification of every reported technical opinion.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا من حيث إنها موجودة أو أصوات
records.english: Expressions are not studied here simply because they exist, are sounds, are accidents rather than substances, are necessary or possible, or are temporally enduring or successive. They are considered only in the respect relevant to logical teaching and signification. The note prefers this pedagogical restriction to treating words themselves as an essential component of logic.
records.editorial: Distinguishes object studied under a qualification from word as physical object.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أراد بالعلم العلم الحصولي المنقسم إلى التصور والتصديق
records.english: Knowledge here means acquired or representational knowledge divided into conception and assent. Verbal signs may therefore indicate simple or compound meanings, including incomplete possessive and attributive combinations and complete performative or reportable clauses.
records.editorial: The different kinds of compound expression are listed by rhetorical and logical function.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: إن كان منشأ الحيثية المذكورة في تعريف الدلالة وضع الواضع
records.english: When the signifying relation arises because a convention-maker has assigned a sign to a meaning, the indication is conventional (*waḍʿiyya*). The note also mentions different pronunciations of *ḥasab* depending on whether it follows a preposition, with a rare poetic alternative.
records.editorial: Conventional causation is not the same thing as a rational proof from an effect.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لكونها منسوبة إلى الوضع الذي له مدخل
records.english: It is called conventional because the establishment of a sign–meaning assignment contributes to that kind of signification.
records.editorial: Very short source gloss.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: وهي الخطوط والعقود والإشارات والنصب
records.english: Nonverbal conventional signs include writing, finger-count arrangements, bodily signals and erected markers. Written letters may designate an individual, fingers may encode numerical ranks, a doorkeeper's gesture may indicate whether to enter, and a road marker may direct travellers. In each case the sign works through a learned convention.
records.editorial: Four types distinguished with examples.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, quoting al-Sayyid al-Sharīf
records.arabicLemma: وإن كان بسبب اقتضاء الطبع
records.english: Natural verbal signification may be attributed to the speaker's disposition to produce a sound when a state occurs, to a state that naturally calls forth that sound, or to the hearer's instinctive understanding of it without knowing a convention. Al-Sayyid al-Sharīf objects that the hearer-focused account does not cleanly distinguish natural from rational indication, because neither requires knowledge of a word assignment. A defensible definition therefore needs an account of the nature producing or prompting the sign, not merely the listener's arrival at a meaning.
records.editorial: Argument includes disputed alternatives; the passage's wording and attribution need a second Arabic translation pass.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله كدلالة أح أح
records.english: A spontaneously uttered “aḥ, aḥ” is used as an example of naturally indicating pain. Different pronunciations of the interjection are compared with expressions such as “akh,” “uff” and “āh,” which can convey suffering, vexation or grief. The gloss records earlier disagreements about the vocalisation and the corresponding emotional state.
records.editorial: Cross-page lexical alternatives and vocalisations require full source/audio philology.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله ودلالة سرعة النبض على الحمى
records.english: A rapid pulse indicating fever is proposed as *nonverbal natural signification*. Some earlier classifications allowed only conventional and rational forms of nonverbal indication. The writer defends an additional natural class through facial flushing, paling from fear, bodily movement in response to music, and characteristic movements of animals. The same sign can also support a rational inference if a necessary causal link is known. But a person can recognise the sign through habituated experience of nature without knowing such a link. Thus the classification depends in part on *why the observer moves from sign to signified*, not solely on the sign's physical shape.
records.editorial: A complex overlap of causal and habituated indication; source expressly challenges a five-type-only taxonomy.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, reporting al-Sayyid al-Sharīf
records.arabicLemma: كدلالة لفظ ديز المسموع من وراء الجدار
records.english: The meaningless sound *dīz* heard from behind a wall indicates the existence of a speaker by rational inference, not through a convention that assigns it a lexical meaning. A meaningful utterance could likewise indicate the speaker, but a beginner might confuse that rational inference with the word's conventional signification. The wall makes the point vivid: the speaker is not directly seen. Hearing a visible speaker also gives rational evidence of that person, but it is overshadowed by simultaneous visual perception. The presence of direct sight does not logically remove the sound's evidential function.
records.editorial: Historical example includes a cross-page discussion of visibility, sound and rational inference; English rendered as an analysis, not a fully collation-certified source note.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: هذه الأقسام حاصلة من ضرب الاثنين
records.english: The conventional, natural and rational types cross with verbal and nonverbal signs to produce six classified kinds. Their exhaustiveness is supported by surveying cases, not a strict contradiction-based proof that no additional relation is possible. By contrast, conventional verbal signification divided into whole, part and external concomitant is treated as exhaustive by conceptual disjunction.
records.editorial: Distinguishes an empirical classification from an alleged rationally exhaustive partition.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: بخلاف الدلالة الطبعية والعقلية فإنها غير منضبطة
records.english: Natural and rational signs vary with different dispositions, understandings, times and circumstances and are therefore not as uniformly regulated as conventional sign assignments.
records.editorial: Do not interpret variability as lack of any causal regularity.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, quoting Quṭb al-Dīn
records.arabicLemma: قوله وهي تنقسم
records.english: A definition of conventional verbal signification is proposed: when a sound is uttered, its assigned meaning is understood *because the listener knows the assignment*. The last condition excludes natural signs, whose comprehension does not depend on learned convention, and rational signs such as hearing a person behind a wall, which indicates a speaker even to someone who does not know the word's meaning. The author treats the relevant logical signification as a general relation, not a meaning occasionally inferred from a special context. Grammarians and jurists, by contrast, may also attend to context-dependent ordinary usage. The gloss explains that saying “knowledge of its assignment” avoids limiting the definition to whole-meaning signification alone.
records.editorial: Quṭb al-Dīn's quoted explanation crosses several technical definitions; a compact rendering, not full independently checked translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: كدلالة لفظ الإنسان على الحيوان الناطق
records.english: The expression “human” signifies the *whole* assigned meaning “rational animal.” The word “whole” excludes an accidental reading in which a part of the assigned meaning would be confused with the entire conventional signification.
