records.editorial: Example of muṭābaqa and its distinctness from taḍammun.

records.speaker: Source note without independent signature
records.arabicLemma: كدلالة الإنسان على الحيوان وحده أو على الناطق وحده
records.english: The word “human” indicates one constituent of its assigned meaning, such as animality alone or rationality alone. This is signification by inclusion (*taḍammun*), not by the whole assigned meaning.
records.editorial: Source item ends before numbered 21, which crosses to p192.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (signature before 22)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو على ما هو خارج عنه لازم له
records.english:
The third signification is a word's indicating something outside its assigned meaning but necessarily associated with it. The word “human,” for example, may indicate the capacity to laugh. The three species are called *muṭābaqa* because the word agrees with its full assigned meaning, *taḍammun* because the signified part lies *within* that meaning, and *iltizām* because the external item accompanies it. In each case the name transfers from the explanatory relation to the resulting indication. The word *iltizām* is chosen over *luzūm*, according to the glossator, to suggest an especially strong connection.

The commentator warns that these descriptions require the qualification “under that aspect” (*min ḥaythu huwa kadhālik*). Otherwise the same indication could be assigned to several species whenever one ambiguous expression is independently assigned to a whole, to one of its parts, and to an external correlate. Suppose the word is assigned independently to both the whole and the part. Its indicating the part **as an assigned meaning in its own right** is by correspondence, but indicating that identical part **as a constituent of the wider assigned meaning** is by inclusion. Similarly, a word separately assigned to a consequent can indicate it by correspondence, whereas the same item considered as the consequent of another assigned meaning is indicated by implication. The bare object indicated does not determine the kind; the *respect in which it is indicated* does.

The intended passage is a division pointing toward definitions, not a fully developed independent definition of each kind. The source therefore allows the accustomed contextual qualifications to remain implicit.
records.editorial: Long note p191–192 with multiple complex counterexamples; not fully word-for-word, source translation marked PARTIAL pending clause alignment.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله في الدلالة الالتزامية
records.english:
A word cannot indicate *every* thing external to its assigned meaning; otherwise one finite expression would signify infinitely many unrelated objects. Implicative signification must therefore have an additional condition, namely an association of the right kind between what the word primarily signifies and the external item.

Whole-meaning signification and contained-part signification require no corresponding further condition beyond knowing the lexical assignment. Someone who knows that a word was assigned to several meanings can understand the several meanings when the word is uttered, although the speaker may intend only one. Likewise a complex assigned meaning gives access to its constituents. Conventional indication is not identical with the speaker's current intention: the hearer may understand meanings which the speaker did not intend. Nor does this produce an infinity of significations, since no finite word is assigned independently to infinitely many meanings, and no finite assigned meaning has infinitely many constituents in the relevant sense.

Implicative signification differs because there may be indefinitely many external objects. The requirement of a sufficiently clear concomitance prevents taking every causal, accidental or merely possible association as something actually implied by the word. The discussion turns on the difference between *an association which can be discovered with further thought* and one that is immediately available through the understanding of the assigned meaning.
records.editorial: Q192 contains full argument with several qualifications; first-pass reasoning is rendered but not a photographic clause-by-clause transcription, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Jalāl al-Dīn
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولا بد من اللزوم عقلا
records.english: An intellectually necessary connection must be such that the accompanying meaning cannot be omitted when the relevant original meaning is conceived—for example, the relation between blindness and sight, where blindness is a privation specified by sight. The author points to Qurʾānic usages that predicate blindness of the eyes or hearts to show the conventional availability of this comparison. Quarrelling over the example itself does not resolve the general definition of implicative indication.
records.editorial: Short historical example; Qurʾānic language and precise account of blindness remain distinct from empirical optics.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله سواء كان هذا اللزوم الذهني عقلا
records.english: The wording may indicate that implicative signification requires mental concomitance in the broad sense, whether established by reason or by settled linguistic custom. Another commentator proposes reading the two expressions as deliberately reporting rival schools: some require rational concomitance, while others admit customary or mental association. If so, the wording would not disclose the author's own preference. The present glossator regards the broad interpretation as more apparent, especially in view of other works by the author.
records.editorial: Alternative interpretation of a reported doctrinal disjunction, not a source-level variant.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله كالبصر بالنسبة إلى العمى
records.english:
An objection says that “sight” is part of the *meaning* of “blindness”; therefore its indication should be by inclusion (*taḍammun*) rather than implication (*iltizām*). The reply analyses blindness as **privation qualified by a relation to sight**, not the conjunction of “privation” and “sight” as two independent constituents. The relation is included; the second relatum, sight, remains external. One cannot apprehend this qualified privation without apprehending the sight in relation to which it is privation.

The source challenges the example from ordinary and Qurʾānic predications such as “the eyes became blind,” apparently treating “blindness” as a state applicable to eyes without an additional figurative indicator. An answer notes that such predication itself supplies the very context which identifies sight as the relevant positive counterpart. The argument illustrates the distinction between an incomplete relational expression and the relatum to which it refers.
records.editorial: Q193 note includes objections about Qurʾānic predication; some intermediate phrasing not independently collated; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Anonymous note quoting Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قال الشيخ محمد على بعد الجواب عن التوهم
records.english: It is surprising that one investigator accepts the answer just offered concerning blindness and sight, yet treats the use of “supplication” (*duʿāʾ*) for “mercy” as naming a whole by one of its parts. Supplication is a *request for* mercy, not the compound “request and mercy.” The thing requested is related to the act of requesting, but is not thereby a constituent of the act itself.
records.editorial: Brief comparison of external relatum vs part of a definition. Authorship follows citation, not whole-volume metadata.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله إذ لا شك ان الدلالة الوضعية على جزء المسمى
records.english:
The author says that conventionally indicating a part of a named meaning or one of its external concomitants depends on indicating the named meaning itself. A thing can be recognised *as part* only in relation to its whole, and a concomitant *as external to* something only in relation to the thing it accompanies. Hence *taḍammun* and *iltizām* depend, in this respect, on *muṭābaqa*.

One proposed syllogism runs: inclusion and implication require an assigned meaning; assignment requires corresponding signification; therefore inclusion and implication require corresponding signification. Another argument takes the two indirect species as subordinate to whole-meaning indication. The glossator questions what this subordination means. If it means later occurrence in *time*, a constituent may be apprehended before the whole, and the positive term involved in a privation may be understood before the privation. If it means the *speaker's principal purpose* in establishing the lexical assignment, one can sometimes arrive only at part of the intended goal without arriving at the whole, so purpose-subordination alone does not secure logical entailment.

The critic adds that a word may be uttered with a contextual indicator directing the speaker's intention toward a part or an external concomitant rather than toward the entire assigned meaning. This does not necessarily abolish the underlying word's conventional correspondence; it suppresses the *intention* to use that correspondence. The underlying distinction between signification and what the speaker wishes to communicate becomes central.

A further test considers the verb as traditionally analysed into action, time and relation to an agent. If one hears a finite verb without an expressed agent, is the action understood while the whole complex is not? One reply posits an implicitly supplied agent; a second denies that an isolated ungrammatical verb use provides the right example; a third rejects the premise that the agent relation forms a constituent of the verb's assigned meaning. These alternatives prevent the example from proving that partial indication independently occurs without any corresponding indication.
records.editorial: Cross-page long note; the full Arabic includes more qualifications than this first-pass translation. Explicitly PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: اعلم انه اختلف كلماتهم في تفسير الدلالات
records.english:
The sources define the three kinds of conventional verbal signification in two different ways. According to the majority, a word signifies its full real assigned meaning by correspondence, a constituent by inclusion, and an external correlate by implication, whether or not the speaker intends that signification. Another school requires the word to be **used for and primarily intended to signify its assigned meaning**; part and concomitant signification are then subordinate to that primary use. On the latter account a word used directly for a constituent is no longer called signification by inclusion but, relative to that use, by correspondence.

The necessity of correspondence for inclusion and implication is straightforward under the second definition: the primary use of the assigned whole is built into the specification. Under the majority's definition it is less obvious, because someone may use a word in its part or concomitant under a familiar convention, and no primary whole-meaning intention is present. The principal commentary's phrase “even in supposition” is introduced as the response. The source closes by noting that the point cannot be exhausted in this short context.
records.editorial: Q194–195 report of rival definitions; analysis abbreviated, not certified full translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: مثال الأول الانسان إذا اشتهر في الحيوان فقط
records.english: An example of the first case is the word “human” becoming conventionally familiar as indicating only “animal” or only “rational.” An example of the second is the word becoming familiar as an expression for “laughing.”
records.editorial: Brief exemplification from note28.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولا عكس
records.english: The reverse dependence does not hold. A word can signify its complete assigned meaning without giving its listener any actual understanding of the constituents or external concomitants individually. The assigned meaning may itself be simple and lack the relevant constituent altogether, or no specially intelligible external correlate may be available. Thus neither inclusion nor implication follows from the mere fact of correspondence.
records.editorial: The contrast is the possible absence of part/concomitant indication, not a new independent lexicon.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.20 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: أي لا عقلا ولا عرفا
records.english: That is: no concomitance, whether by reason or by accepted custom.
records.editorial: A very short independent printed note; completeness here reflects source length.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله فيتحقق حينئذ المطابقة بدون التضمن
records.english:
If an assigned meaning has no parts, correspondence can exist without inclusion. If there is no suitably evident rational or customary concomitant, correspondence can exist without implication. The author questions whether these statements demonstrate actual absence or merely the *possibility* of absence. Showing that something might fail to have a concomitant does not yet prove there is any real case where it fails. Possibility alone does not imply occurrence.

The example of a point or unit is offered as a simple meaning with no parts, defeating an alleged necessary connection between correspondence and inclusion. For implication, one argument appeals to introspection: we often apprehend an object while not simultaneously thinking of another, contrary to the proposal that every apprehension automatically entails an accompanying apprehension. The glossator notes that this requires careful formulation and independent justification.

A second argument says that if every thing necessarily came with a further intelligible consequence, we would need to grasp an infinite series of consequences at once: from the original thing to its necessary correlate, thence to that correlate's own correlate, and so on without end. The commentator replies that the series might close by mutual implication, as in fatherhood and sonship; reciprocal semantic linkage is not a vicious circle of epistemic dependence. Moreover, an infinite sequence of *actual objects* does not establish that each is simultaneously conceived.

A further response groups a thing with its correlate and asks whether the resulting *whole* has another necessary correlate. The glossator objects that conceiving a thing and conceiving its correlate separately does not necessarily entail conceiving the pair *as a combined whole*. It would be a fallacy to pass without argument from jointly available notions to explicit apprehension of their relation.
records.editorial: Long two-page logic of non-entailment, logical possibility vs actual example, and regress. Substantial selective rendering, but not full source translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ولو كان له معنى مركب
records.english:
The next issue is whether inclusion implies implicative signification or vice versa. If a word's assigned meaning is composite yet lacks a separate apprehensible external correlate, the word may indicate a part without implication. Conversely a word assigned to a simple meaning may indicate an external concomitant without indicating any part. The sun and light are cited as a possible example, though the relation depends on how each is conceived.

An opponent argues that whenever a complex whole and one of its parts are understood as such, the relation of composition must also be grasped, and composition lies outside the assigned meaning; hence inclusion would entail implication. The reply distinguishes apprehending an object which happens to be a whole from *apprehending that object under the relation of being a whole*. The latter can make composition explicit, but the former need not. One may apprehend a complex without expressly considering the unity and parts qua unity and parts.

The same problem applies to the relation between *mūṭābaqa*, *taḍammun* and *iltizām* when definitions are written without their aspect-qualifiers. Since an object can stand in different semantic relations under different lexical assignments, any universal entailment must hold under the correctly specified respects, not simply because the same item can be described as a part and as a correlate in different constructions.
records.editorial: Long note p196–197; source includes additional objections/answers about parts; kept PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: أي لا من طرف التضمن ولا من طرف الالتزام
records.english: That is, no necessary implication follows in either direction: not from indication by inclusion to indication by concomitance, nor from indication by concomitance to indication by inclusion. The author leaves these relations unstated because the earlier cases provide enough information for a thoughtful learner to infer them.
records.editorial: Short source explanation, not a new formal proof.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما لم يقل واللفظ كما عبر به البعض
records.english: The author avoids saying “and the expression” without qualification because that would make the subsequent definition of simple and compound terms apply to meaningless utterances, which are not technical simple terms; likewise signs that have meanings only by natural response or accidental association do not enter the intended conventional verbal classification.
records.editorial: Source distinguishes deliberate assignment from natural/rational signs.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما فسر بذلك دفعا لما ربما يتوهم
records.english: The division into simple and compound is not being applied to every object called a “sign” or to the entire earlier sixfold classification. It applies specifically to a *conventionally assigned expression*. Without that restriction some nonverbal signs, such as mere gestures and inscriptions taken under another respect, would be incorrectly forced into the simple/compound lexical division. The expression assigned a meaning for syntactic combination is likewise not the object of the present classification unless that assigned meaning is considered.
records.editorial: Correctly restricts the type of sign to which the division applies.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان أريد بجزء منه الدلالة على جزء معناه
records.english:
The definition of a compound expression says that a part of its wording is *intended to signify a part of its meaning*. What kind of signification is meant? Al-Kātibī and others specify signification by correspondence (*muṭābaqa*); inclusion or implication alone is not enough. Otherwise a word might be compound under its whole assigned meaning while simple under a merely included or external associated meaning. Opponents reply that it is acceptable for one word to be simple in one linguistic assignment and compound in another, as in “ʿAbd Allāh” used as a proper name versus the possessive phrase “servant of God.”

The respondent distinguishes this familiar ambiguity across *different linguistic assignments* from the proposed competition of two kinds of signification under one and the same assignment. Giving priority to the meaning indicated by correspondence has a rationale: any composition recognised under a contained or implied sense can be related to the whole assigned sense, while composition of the whole need not require composition of each included or associated meaning. Others reverse this reasoning for simplicity, but the reply says that “compound” is a positive notion and “simple” a privative one; in a classification of this kind, the positive mark of composition has explanatory priority.

A major objection concerns finite verbs. If a verb's meaning includes action, time and relation to an agent, do its material letters signify the action while its vocalic pattern signifies time, making an ordinary verb a compound expression? One answer distinguishes an audible, successively arranged part from a merely formal pattern or grammatical configuration; an inflectional pattern is not independently heard as a separate sequence of sound in the way two words are. But then hidden pronominal subjects in imperatives seem to be genuine meaning-bearing constituents without an independently audible component. The response allows an expression that is hearable *in principle* or mentally restored in the grammatical analysis, as “strike [you]!” includes an understood subject.

The glossator criticizes the answer: if the vocalic form is not a meaningful part of the verb at all, the earlier argument assumed what it must prove. A more coherent position, he claims, holds that the verb is a single conventional unit whose assigned meaning is a simple event-form abstracted from action, time and relation, rather than the aggregate of three separately designated constituents. Under that view the apparent objection to the compound/simple division does not arise in the same form.

Why, nevertheless, present “compound” before “simple” when the simple precedes the compound in nature? The answer invokes the contrast of possession and privation: “compound” affirms a positive feature and “simple” denotes its absence. Since the definition is made through this conceptual opposition, the positive notion may appropriately come first even if an elementary simple expression is naturally prior to an articulated compound.
records.editorial: LONG three-page technical discussion. This is a structured first-pass rendering of the argument, not full clause-paired Arabic; remain PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: المراد من الجزء هو الجزء المسموع المرتب في السمع
records.english: The relevant component of an expression is what can be heard and ordered in hearing, actually or in grammatical supposition. This avoids counting the purely formal grammatical pattern of a finite verb as a separate audible word, while still allowing an implicitly understood subject in an imperative to be restored in analysis. Yet a contrary view says that if form were no part of the verb as a sign at all, one would fail to explain how its form can determine its temporal meaning. Further difficulty arises from audible prefixes in present-tense verbs and elements marking mutual participation: their segments carry meaning but are not always treated as independently compound words. The logicians' concept of one simple term need not coincide in every case with the grammarian's classification of one morphologically inflected word.
records.editorial: Cross-page condensed argument, source note is longer. Remains PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله والثالث ان يدل جزء لفظه على جزء معناه
records.english: The original Aristotelian definition of a compound was commonly stated as an expression whose part indicates a part of its meaning. Later writers added that this indication must be **intended**, because a multiword expression such as “ʿAbd Allāh” may be used as a single proper name without intending its components separately to signify a servant and God. The logician's attention to semantic unity explains why this case differs from a grammatical division based on word count alone.
records.editorial: The historical reference to Aristotle is a report, not an independently checked translation of the Organon.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله الرابع ان يكون هذه الدلالة مرادة
records.english:
Meaning-signification may occur even when the speaker does not intend it. A person familiar with an ambiguous word automatically apprehends several assigned senses when hearing it, even if the speaker intends only one. Why, then, make intention part of the definition of a compound expression? The qualification concerns the **intended signification of one part toward one constituent** in the use of the whole expression, not the psychological presence of every possible meaning.

The note reports an important dispute. Avicenna in the *Shifāʾ* is quoted as saying that a word does not signify by its mere sound; its signification is related to what the speaker intends. If the word *ʿayn* is intended for a spring it indicates the spring; if for a coin, it indicates that. Without any intention, some logicians hesitate to call an uninterpreted sound a word. Al-Ṭūsī is similarly cited for treating conventional verbal signification as attached to the speaker's intention of the utterance.

Later commentators strongly oppose this. Knowledge of a lexical assignment ordinarily makes a hearer conceive the assigned meaning whether or not the speaker intends it. A person who knows several senses of *ʿayn* can mentally access each on hearing it, while a contextual indicator is needed to identify which one was intended. The glossator proposes that much of the dispute is verbal: one school calls only the passage to the *intended* meaning “signification,” the other calls the broader automatic passage to known assigned senses “signification.” Both sides acknowledge that understood meanings and a particular speaker's intention are not the same fact.
records.editorial: Historical Avicenna–Ṭūsī vs later tradition. Condensed from long p200–201 material; PARTIAL, verify quotations separately.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله لكن هذه الدلالة غير مقصودة
records.english: If “intended” in defining compound terms means *actually intended at the moment*, even ordinary compound expressions not now used would fall into the simple category. If it means *capable of being intended*, a proper name composed of words might be counted compound simply because its components could be used independently under another assignment. The proper restriction is the ability of a constituent to signify its part **when the whole expression is used to signify this particular assigned meaning**.
records.editorial: Distinguishes actual current purpose from use-relative ability to signify.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: فان معناه حينئذ الماهية الانسانية مع التشخص
records.english: If a phrase such as “rational animal” names a particular individual, its signified meaning is the human essence together with individuation. The component “animal” can still correspond to one part of that complex when the phrase is analysed under its descriptive assignment. But that does not settle how the whole is being used as an actual proper name. The intended assignment must be fixed before deciding whether its parts make it compound.
records.editorial: Exact distinction of descriptive content and proper-name use; source note crosses p201→202.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يحتاج الى انضمام لفظ آخر إليه في الإفادة
records.english: A complete utterance conveys its intended information without needing another expression, as “Zayd is standing” does. A lone “Zayd” or “standing” generally requires something else. “The hearer can stop” may refer to the speaker's cessation, the listener's cessation or both, depending on the adopted convention.
records.editorial: Short note on completeness of propositional speech.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان احتمل الصدق والكذب
records.english: A report is a complete expression **of a kind capable of truth or falsehood**, not one whose actual truth and falsity are both genuinely open once every fact has been determined. “The whole is greater than the part” is necessarily true, and “the part is greater than the whole” necessarily false, but both are reports because their predicative form can be evaluated for agreement or disagreement with reality. The criterion abstracts from the particular fact and considers the statement as an assertion.
records.editorial: Modal versus kind-level aptitude for truth and falsity distinguished.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي بأحدهما كما يدل عليه عطف كاذب بأو
records.english: The phrase means “capable of one of the two,” not actually possessing both truth and falsity. The disjunction is exclusive in the relevant actual assessment.
records.editorial: A short clarification of *aw*.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: اعلم ان الانشاء اما ان لا يدل على طلب الشيء بالوضع
records.english: Nonassertoric utterances (*inshāʾ*) divide into those not conventionally signalling a request, such as expressions of hope, calling, surprise and certain oaths, and those that do signal a request. If what is sought is an item of knowledge in the mind, it is an interrogative. If it is the occurrence or nonoccurrence of something outside the mind, the form is a command or prohibition when uttered from superiority, a request between equals (*iltimās*) when on equal standing, and a supplication (*suʾāl*) when uttered humbly.
records.editorial: A source-specific classification of nonassertoric speech and relative authority.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.21 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان كان الجزء الثاني قيدا للأول
records.english: The question is whether the second member is **taken as restricting** the first. It may be grammatically capable of acting as a restriction without being treated as such in this particular expression. Restrictive compound forms include genitive, descriptive/adjectival and related constructions.
records.editorial: Emphasizes intentional grammatical consideration.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله غلام زيد ... انما اورد ثلاثة امثلة
records.english: The examples “Zayd's servant,” a modified noun, and “standing in the house” show that a restrictive compound may arise through possession, an adjective or a governing relation. It is not limited to the first two kinds.
records.editorial: Brief argument from the three examples.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان لم يكن الثاني قيدا للأول
records.english: “Not restrictive” means that the second component is not *considered* a qualifier of the first, even if it could serve that function in another construction. The decisive feature is the current interpretation, not whether the example happens to include a preposition or a numeral.
records.editorial: Note crosses Q202→203.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله في الدار وخمسة عشر
records.english: Two nonrestrictive examples illustrate different reasons. In “in the house,” the particle *fī* indicates a specific relation rather than a generic absolute item which the following noun could narrow; “the house” supplies its relational endpoint. In “fifteen,” the word “five” may have a more general application by itself, but combining it with “ten” does not restrict that first term in the manner of an adjective modifying a noun; it forms a composite numeral. These cases also vary as to whether the second expression determines a sense of the first, whether the first is a particle or noun, and whether it governs the second.
records.editorial: The source also argues against restricting nonrestrictive compounds to a name+particle pattern; wording condensed, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: وذلك لكون معناه مستقلا في الملاحظة
records.english: A noun’s meaning is independent in consideration. Unlike a particle, it can be apprehended as a meaning in its own right without the two related terms being supplied first.
records.editorial: Short gloss on the logician's division of words.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: الأولى أن يجيء بأحرف
records.english: The writer would more naturally have said “letters” using the plural of paucity (*aḥruf*), since the counted number is ten or fewer and Arabic usage customarily employs a paucity plural in that context.
records.editorial: Grammatical style criticism, not logically necessary terminology.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: انما سمى الفتح فتحا
records.english: The vowel *fatḥa* is so named because one produces it by opening the mouth.
records.editorial: Single-sentence lexical observation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: الغرض من وصف المادة لكونها موضوعة
records.english:
The word's material component must be described as conventionally assigned and available to grammatical variation in order to exclude a familiar objection. If the morphological pattern alone indicates time, then a noun of the same phonetic pattern as a past verb should also indicate time, contrary to usage. If the pattern needs the material letters to cooperate, why do expressions such as “yesterday,” “now” and “tomorrow” not become verbs simply because their material and phonetic arrangements indicate time?

The reply restricts the definition to a material base which is itself a conventionally designated item and subject to morphological operation, not any letters or pattern whose arrangement happens to suggest a time. The verb form is not to be identified with every occurrence of the same vowel sequence; lexical assignment matters.
records.editorial: The note gives examples and counterexamples in historical morphology; substantially interpreted, not full line-by-line translation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أما الأول فلانتفاء الوضع
records.english: The former case lacks the relevant conventional assignment; the latter lacks the relevant capacity for morphological variation. The two conditions therefore exclude the two proposed counterexamples for different reasons.
records.editorial: Short cross-reference to note54.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: انما سميت بها لأن الكلم في الأصل الجرح
records.english: The word is associated with *kalām* in its older sense of wounding. A verb indicates a time-related occurrence that changes and passes, so it is likened to something that wounds the mind by its changing signification. This is a rhetorical etymology reported in the gloss, not a verified historical derivation.
records.editorial: Source employs a traditional etymological analogy.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفي عرف النحاة فعل
records.english:
The main commentator's words seem to suggest that the logical category called *kalima* corresponds exactly to what grammarians call a *fiʿl*. An objector points out that grammarians classify defective verbs such as *kāna* among verbs, whereas logicians sometimes treat them as relational particles. Conversely grammarians classify “names of verbs” (*asmāʾ al-afʿāl*) as nouns, even when a logician treats their meaning as a time-related predication.

The reply is that the author need not affirm an equivalence in both directions. He could mean only that the items classed as *kalimāt* under his logical definition fall among what grammarians call verbs, without claiming that every grammatical verb is a logical *kalima*. Another response questions the premise that names of verbs meet the author's strict criterion that the expression's form, rather than a separately assigned name, indicates time. The dispute thus concerns the conditions for a classification and the direction of a claimed implication, not simply the labels adopted by two professions.
records.editorial: Long Q203→204 note with competing definitions; PARTIAL pending Arabic source collation.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله وان لم يستقل في الدلالة
records.english: A particle does not signify independently: *min* and *ilā* become intelligible as beginning and end when attached to expressions like “I travelled from Basra to Kufa.” Defective “existential” verbs such as *kāna* can resemble particles insofar as they primarily express a relation which cannot be understood without its two terms; unlike a simple particle, however, they may also convey a temporal determination. The word *adāt* is used because such items are instruments for combining expressions, while the grammatical term *ḥarf* recalls their occupying the edge of a sentence rather than constituting its main element.
records.editorial: A source-defined functional distinction, not identity of logicians' and grammarians' parts of speech.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يرد عليه أن ضمائر الفصل والأفعال الناقصة أدوات
records.english: The proposed identification of the logical particle with the grammarian's *ḥarf* fails without qualification: separating pronouns and defective verbs can function as logical instruments while grammarians categorise the former as nouns and the latter as verbs.
records.editorial: Counterexamples to cross-discipline equivalence.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.21 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وأيضا مفعول مطلق
records.english: The small word *ayḍan* (“also”) is examined because it may signal that the following divisions apply to the entire class of simple expressions, not just to the noun as one type. Yet terms like proper name, univocal term and gradated term are not naturally ascribed to particles whose meanings require another term, or to verbs whose forms and time-significations alter with inflection. An answer treats the following divisions as applying to the simple expression under a relevant restriction—primarily to its nominal type. The principal commentator's “reflect” may be meant to remind the reader of that restriction.
records.editorial: A reported critical problem of division scope; longer alternatives remain, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله مفعول مطلق لفعل محذوف
records.english: *Ayḍan* may be a cognate accusative governed by an omitted verb, or a circumstantial expression with its agent and owner suppressed. Its idiomatic use presupposes two things standing in some agreement while each can, in principle, be understood apart from the other. An isolated occurrence such as “Zayd came also” without an understood second comparison does not meet that condition.
records.editorial: One grammatical analysis of the connective *ayḍan*.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بيان كونه إشارة إليه
records.english: The particle signals a return to a preceding division. A return to the same object being divided conveys the sense of return more strongly than merely shifting to a new subject.
records.editorial: Explanation of the phrase's discourse function.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: حال من الاسم على تأويله بالنكرة عند سيبويه
records.english: The phrase can function as a circumstance (*ḥāl*) of a definite noun if the noun is understood under an indefinite description. Other grammarians treat a mentally known definite as semantically indefinite in the relevant respect, dispensing with the transformation; others posit a cognate accusative of an omitted action, or a temporal circumstantial adjunct meaning “in the condition of being single.” The objection is that the genitive construction ordinarily produces determination rather than indefiniteness. The writer favours the straightforward circumstantial interpretation and questions whether an overt indefinite reconstruction is needed.
records.editorial: Records several grammarians' parsings in compressed form; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وفيه بحث
records.english:
A general class may be divided into species without every species containing *every* further subdivision of the whole. Therefore it is not formally necessary that “proper,” “univocal” and “gradated” occur among nouns, verbs and particles separately; it might be enough for the subdivisions to cover the whole collection.

The glossator replies that this misses the objection. If verbs and particles are genuinely members of the broader subject being divided but cannot belong to *any* of the listed resulting classes, then the division is not exhaustive. It does not help to say that not every category must be found in every species. The proposed repair restricts the subject to simple expressions *whose meanings admit the relevant univocal, equivocal or multiple senses*; in the current technical usage these are nominal expressions with independently apprehensible meanings. Verbs and particles, considered as such, do not meet this further condition and are outside the effective division.

The response also denies that the general class must be constrained by a condition never declared in the original wording. The presence of a qualifying “if,” and the fact that the later distinctions require one kind of nominal meaning, are offered as evidence for the restriction. This is a debate about whether an unstated type restriction is contextually licensed.
records.editorial: Long Q205→206 source about exhaustive classification and type restriction; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.22 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله الفعل والحرف اذا كانا متحدي المعنى
records.english: “One in meaning” here means that the material elements of the verb or particle are used in one assigned sense rather than as an ambiguous word with several independent senses.
records.editorial: Single-sentence reported clarification.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.22 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: وجه التأمل أن مناط الكلية والجزئية باعتبار المعنى
records.english: Universality and particularity concern the **meaning**, not the expression considered merely as a sound. A particle's meaning is dependent, and a verb under its complete assigned signification is not ordinarily presented as an independent class-concept in the relevant way; neither is automatically universal or particular under the nomenclature of the proposed noun division.
records.editorial: Source-specific criterion for logical universality.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ليس الغرض من اتحاد المعنى اتفاقه مع اللفظ في العدد
records.english: “Unity of meaning” does not mean numerical agreement between one word and one individual. Different proper names may be assigned to the same individual while each remains a proper name. The unity at issue is of the relevant denoted meaning under the adopted consideration.
records.editorial: Distinguishes numerical count of labels from unit of meaning.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm with separate Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī continuation
records.arabicLemma: اعلم أنه لا بد لتحقيق الحال من تفصيل المقال
records.english:
For a conventional assignment to be made, the assigner must have some conception of the item for which an expression is selected. If the item conceived is particular and the word is assigned to that particular, the act of assignment is specific and the meaning assigned specific. If a universal is conceived and a word assigned to that universal, both the act of assignment and what is assigned may be general. A third possibility conceives a universal, then assigns the sign to the particular instances under that universal without separately conceiving each in detail. The act of assignment is general in its basis, while the assigned meanings are particular.

The source uses this distinction to debate pronouns, demonstratives, relative pronouns and expressions made definite through the article. Some treat such expressions as general designation for a universal meaning, others as general assignment to particular referents. Under the latter, numerous applications do not make one common type-concept the immediate assigned referent of each occurrence. The principal author’s qualification “by assignment” is said to exclude these ambiguous expressions from an overly broad definition of the proper name. The analysis, however, depends on whether unity refers to the assigned type or to the referents taken under individual acts of reference.
records.editorial: Cross-page very technical historical waḍʿ debate, abbreviated; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وهاهنا كلام وهو أن المراد بالمعنى
records.english:
The expression “meaning” in the division of simple terms can refer either to what the word was **originally assigned to** or to what the word is **actually used to convey**, including transferred and figurative meanings. The glossator argues that a problem follows whichever alternative is adopted.

If the original assigned meaning alone counts, literal and figurative uses of a word do not form a type with multiple originally assigned meanings, since figurative transfer is not another primary lexical assignment. If current conveyed meanings count, demonstratives, univocal words and gradated words will also have many applications and could fall under the “multiple meanings” class. The qualification “by assignment” would then fail to perform its supposed function of excluding them.

One response proposes a rhetorical shift of reference (*istikhdām*): “one in meaning” may mean one original assigned meaning, while “if the meanings are many” may speak of the actual different uses. But the glossator regards this as a costly interpretation, and notes the issue cannot be settled by simply calling the word “meaning” identical through both clauses. The distinction between **designation**, **use**, and **what an utterance is used for here** must remain clear.
records.editorial: Long cross-page source with poetry as examples of rhetorical *istikhdām*; these are not fully rendered, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: أي في قوله وان كثر الخ بعيد
records.english: The qualification is remote in the words “if the meaning is many,” since a word's original assigned meaning in a literal/figurative pair need not itself be multiple.
records.editorial: Source locates a flaw in the alleged rhetorical reconstruction.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لان المستعمل فيه فيها ليس بمتحد بل متكثر
records.english: On the proposed reading of “meaning” as what a word is used for: such meanings may be multiple in proper figurative uses, but then univocal and gradated terms also have many individually applied referents. The restriction to “one meaning” cannot be maintained merely by shifting from assigned meaning to separate applications. A response that the same universal essence is present in all the applications does not settle the problem, since the expressions can also be employed for individual referents, whether directly or by figurative transfer.
records.editorial: Source crosses Q207→208 and explicitly resists the unrestricted used-meaning reading.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله فلا حاجة في إخراجها
records.english:
The qualification “by assignment” may be redundant even if one reads the author's words as concerning original assigned meaning. Demonstratives and related expressions would already be excluded from a personal proper name by the requirement that its assigned sense be particular and individuated. A more sophisticated interpretation shifts reference twice: the earlier “meaning” denotes the assigned universal, while the pronoun and subsequent “particular” refer to its individual uses. That reconstruction might make “by assignment” do some work, but it requires a controlled rhetorical shift of reference.

Two residual difficulties follow. First, an indefinite expression intended to select “some individual or other” may appear to designate one particular under a general assignment, though it is not a proper name. The reply distinguishes inclusive applicability to many together from alternative applicability to one selected from many. Second, proper names can be personal names or names of a *kind*, such as an animal species. A definition restricted to an individuated personal referent appears to omit the latter. It must either include names of kinds among univocal/gradated expressions, contrary to the received naming convention, or accept an unclassified middle.
records.editorial: Long note with second objection about an indefinite *one of* and names of kinds; condensed, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله يكون صدق هذا المعنى الكلي على تلك الأفراد على السوية
records.english:
A *mutawāṭiʾ* universal is predicated equally of its individuals, while a *mushakkik* universal is predicated under priority, strength, perfection or other gradations. Must equality and inequality be real relations between actually existing individuals, or may they be merely imagined? If actually existing individuals are required, universals with only hypothetical or impossible instances would fit neither class. But if arbitrary supposition is sufficient, a thinker could classify a universal as univocal or gradated at will, undermining the familiar determinations that “human” is univocal and “existence” is gradated, and also the rule that a gradated concept is not essential to its subjects.

The reply interprets the assessment as objective but counterfactual: **were the relevant individuals to be instantiated**, would the universal be equally or unequally applicable under its nature? This can be assessed whether those individuals are external, mental, or some external and some mental. The universals therefore do not require actual external exemplification to be classified.

The term *mutawāṭiʾ* recalls agreement or equal application. *Mushakkik* suggests causing uncertainty between univocal application and multiple unrelated meanings, because the concept remains one in origin yet is realised with different degrees.
records.editorial: A full-page philosophical debate, rendered as an analytical first pass and PARTIAL pending line-by-line source comparison.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī (followed by separately introduced ʿAbd al-Raḥīm comment)
records.arabicLemma: قوله يكون صدق هذا المفهوم على بعض
records.english:
Two different gradations should be distinguished. *Awwaliyya* is priority in a causally ordered respect, as existence belongs primarily to the Necessary and only dependently to the contingent. *Awlawiyya* is a greater completeness or fitness of the predication, as existence may be stronger or more established in one subject than another. Temporal anteriority does not by itself count as the priority in question; what matters is an intrinsic or causal precedence of the concept's reality.

The source gives a counterexample to conflating priority with strength: a causally prior item need not be more complete in the same characteristic than what follows it. An independently introduced passage by ʿAbd al-Raḥīm emphasizes that the causal priority must be such that the posterior case cannot occur without the anterior, whereas the difference of strength may go the other way.
records.editorial: Long note + a separately introduced adjacent authorial contribution. The distinct quoted material is summarized here but needs a separate fully transcribed source.

unnumberedFollowing.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, separately introduced Q210
unnumberedFollowing.en: Causal or essential priority is required, not mere earlier occurrence in time. The posterior instance of existence depends on the causally prior instance, but greater strength of existence is not automatically entailed by priority. This is a separately attributed gloss, not part of the numbered source voice.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: هذا اما بسبب ان المفهوم في بعض افراده ذاتي
records.english: The concept may differ across its instances because it is essential to some and accidental to others, or because those instances themselves differ in perfection and deficiency. Such differences can account for a more or less complete predication.
records.editorial: Short source taxonomy of gradation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, followed by quoted al-Taqrīb criticism
records.arabicLemma: قوله ان تفاوتت باولية او اولوية
records.english: The author mentions gradation by priority or greater fittingness “for example,” not, on this reading, because these are the only gradations. Differences of quantity and quality—including more/less and stronger/weaker—may be described separately. A quoted al-Taqrīb writer objects that the two categories may already be broad enough to include them, so adding further kinds need not yield a genuinely new division. The grammatical question is whether “for example” modifies the predicate and whether a suppressed object of quotation must be supplied.
records.editorial: Multiple speakers including al-Taqrīb; source argument abbreviated and PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: مثال الأول كالمقدار بالنسبة إلى من ومنين
records.english: Amount as predicated of one measure and two measures exemplifies a quantitative more-and-less. Whiteness in snow and ivory exemplifies a difference of degree in quality. The first belongs to quantity, the second to quality, according to the reported example.
records.editorial: Examples illustrate different categories of gradation.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: المراد بالوضع الابتدائي
records.english: “Primary assignment” means that the expression is assigned to this meaning independently at the outset, rather than first assigned to another and later transferred to the present meaning through common use. The qualification is intended to distinguish a word assigned separately to several senses from a word which acquired a second use by transfer.
records.editorial: Source definition crosses into p211.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بان يكون موضوعا لكل واحد من تلك المعاني بوضع اخر
records.english: A homonymous expression may have different independent assignments to its meanings, potentially made in different languages or by different speakers, rather than one general assignment to a range of individuals. A word assigned to one sense in Arabic and another in Turkish can illustrate this if both assignments are genuinely established. The case differs from one general assignment covering many individual applications.
records.editorial: Original example uses *nabīdh* across Arabic and Turkish; language-specific assignment needs lexicographic control.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو لا يكون كذلك
records.english: The alternative “not like that” negates a universal qualification: it need not mean that the word is assigned to **none** of the meanings. The broader subject remains a *meaningfully assigned expression*, so total absence of any assignment would be excluded. This is the difference between denial of universality and universal denial.
records.editorial: Historical quantifier-scope distinction, not merely lexical.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, with following separately attributed elaboration
records.arabicLemma: أي مشتركا فيه بالنسبة الى الجميع
records.english: The word is homonymous with respect to the entire set of independently assigned meanings, though in relation to each isolated meaning the designation is specific. The intended meaning on a particular occasion is unclear without a contextual indicator, and thus the utterance is *mujmal* in that respect. A broader subsequent gloss elaborates why several distinct assignments do not automatically make a word unassigned in the alternative case.
records.editorial: Source note closes before a longer new quotation, which needs its own separate source voice.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: قوله كالعين للباصرة
records.english: The eye as the organ of sight is the first meaning given by one lexicographer for the word *ʿayn*. The source lists its feminine gender and plural forms *aʿyān*, *aʿyun* and *ʿuyūn*.
records.editorial: Short lexicographic item, not evidence of first historical assignment.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله وعلى الثاني
records.english:
If a word is not originally assigned to each of its many current uses by separate first assignments, several combinations remain. It might have no assignment to any of them, though this is excluded for an expression actually used with meaning. It might have acquired all through one secondary general assignment, or through several secondary assignments; it may have one primary general assignment applied to many particular contexts; or some uses may be primary and others secondary.

The discussion distinguishes demonstratives and related expressions under old and later theories of conventional assignment, a transferred technical word which underwent several disciplinary transfers, and literal/figurative pairs which continue to be employed in their original and extended meanings. The historical note develops a taxonomy of first versus later designation and of one general versus multiple distinct assignments, not a single simple opposition.
records.editorial: Long Q212–213 note with multiple cases and subcases, condensed and kept PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm
records.arabicLemma: بفتح الميم مصدر ميمي بمعنى التحول
records.english: The term is a verbal noun with fatḥa on the mīm and signifies transfer from one state to another. The reported expression “without doubt” has an omitted predicate; in context it emphasizes that the negation applies to the relevant universal claim and not automatically to every qualified case. The difference is one of scope.
records.editorial: Short lexical and logical scope gloss.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله فان اشتهر في هذا المعنى الثاني
records.english: A word counts as transferred (*manqūl*) when its second use becomes sufficiently familiar to convey its meaning without a contextual indicator. This does not require total extinction of its first use. Making abandonment of the first sense a condition would exclude genuine examples where both remain known.
records.editorial: Distinguishes conventional transfer from total historical obsolescence.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: يعني ان المراد من ترك الاستعمال
records.english:
“Abandonment” of the former use means that in the new specialised usage the earlier meaning is no longer conveyed *literally without contextual indication*. The earlier meaning may remain possible under other contexts. A word like *ṣalāt* can remain available for “supplication,” although in legal usage its dominant, unqualified sense is a prescribed complex of actions. Relative to the original ordinary lexicon the old meaning is literal and the new one figurative or transferred; relative to the second technical register those evaluations can reverse.

The note emphasizes that *manqūl* may still be listed among expressions with multiple uses because the two senses remain available under their respective conventions. The actual condition concerns the immediate meaning a speaker and hearer take without a special indicator **in the current usage-domain**, not whether the former meaning has disappeared everywhere.
records.editorial: Q213→214 technical discussion with quotation; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.24 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله وان لم يستعمل لم يشتهر
records.english: In the contrast between the transferred and the figurative, the second usage has not become so established that it conveys its sense without a contextual indicator. Figurative application exists, but it still needs a sign that the literal assigned meaning is not intended.
records.editorial: Source reports a variant *lam yashta hir* vs *lam yustaʿmal*, not independently collated.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فالحقيقة هو اللفظ المستعمل فيما وضع له
records.english:
A literal expression (*ḥaqīqa*) is one used for what it was assigned to signify under the relevant language or technical convention **in that very respect**. The actual-use requirement excludes an expression not used on any occasion; “for what it was assigned” excludes figurative uses; and “under the relevant convention” distinguishes a word's ordinary sense from an acquired technical sense. The aspect qualification is necessary: one may utter a word that once had the old lexical assignment while employing it in a new technical register, where the meaning is no longer literal in the present communicative setting.

The source also treats the etymology of *ḥaqīqa*: from a form meaning established in its original place, whether understood actively or passively. A disagreement over its feminine suffix follows, including the distinction between an adjective directly modifying a noun and an adjective treated as a substantive. Those morphological details complicate but do not abolish the basic contrast between “fixed in its original assignment” and “carried to another.”
records.editorial: Full Q214 note with multiple etymological/morphological alternatives; condensed and PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله يسمى مجازا
records.english:
*Majāz* is a word used outside the meaning assigned to it under the speaker's current convention, **with a contextual indicator blocking an unqualified literal reading**. Without the last condition *kināya* would also be called metaphor in the same strict sense, even where the literal meaning remains possible. Some add that the use must be linguistically legitimate, thereby excluding accidental mistakes such as pointing to a book and calling it a horse. Whether that extra condition is necessary depends on whether “use” is already understood as competent linguistic use.

The etymological explanation derives *majāz* from traversing or passing beyond a place: the expression goes beyond its original assigned domain. A different etymology likens it to a path by which the hearer reaches a meaning. The writer prefers the first because it preserves the terminological opposition to *ḥaqīqa*, which remains fixed in its original place. The source then distinguishes the **reason a name was originally assigned** from a present-day condition of predication. A person called “Harith” continues to bear the proper name even when he does not plough; a descriptive predicate “plougher” requires current relevance, depending on its grammar.

The literal/figurative difference can also apply to verbs and particles in light of their syntactic complements, not only to isolated noun-stems. Whether a verb's morphological time aspect or a particle's syntactic function itself admits a technical transferred meaning is contested among schools.
records.editorial: Long Q214→215, multiple grammatical/speaker issues; first-pass structured PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: عطف تفسير للعرف الخاص
records.english: The following expression explicates “specialised usage” (*ʿurf khāṣṣ*) rather than introducing an entirely independent class.
records.editorial: Very short grammatical reference.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: ان كان مع ياء النسبة كما في بعض النسخ
records.english: If the word bears the adjectival yāʾ in the variant reported from some copies, the example denotes *members of a specialised convention*. If without that suffix, as in most copies according to the gloss, it denotes the specialised convention itself. This is a source-reported copy variant, NOT a confirmed independent manuscript reading.
records.editorial: Last H-DALALA local numbered note. Qum p216 begins a NEW section titled حواشي المفاهيم, with its own local note1.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: لا يخفى أن هذا الفرق بمجرد الاعتبار
records.english: The distinction in question is due to the perspective under which the same item is considered, like the earlier difference between *ṣidq* and *ḥaqq*. It does not necessarily posit two numerically independent things.
records.editorial: Short programmatic distinction at the beginning of the new H-MAFAHIM section.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (signature in searchable source)
records.arabicLemma: قوله اعلم : ان ما استفيد من اللفظ
records.arabicFullText:
قوله اعلم : ان ما استفيد من اللفظ . . . : لا يخفى ان المفهوم من هذا الكلام ان المفهوم والمعنى متحدان بالذات ، والمعنى على ما عرفوه هو الصورة الذهنية من حيث وضع اللفظ بإزائها فيكون المفهوم أيضا عبارة عن الصورة الذهنية ، فيلزم ان يكون الكلية والجزئية من صفات الصورة وهما من صفات ذي الصورة ويلزم أيضا ان يكون المعتبر في الكلى والجزئي منع تصور الصورة وعدمه والمعتبر منع تصور ذي الصورة وعدمه ولا يدفع ذلك بما ذكره المحقق الشريف في حاشية شرح المطالع بعد قول الشارح : المفهوم هو ما حصل في العقل ، من أن المراد بالحاصل ما من شأنه ان يحصل في العقل سواء حصل بالعقل أولا ، لان الشئ الذي شأنه محصول في الذهن هو الصورة لا ذي الصورة على أن المراد بالحاصل ، الحاصل بالفعل ، لان الكلية والجزئية من العوارض الذهنية فالذي لم يحصل في الذهن بالفعل ليس بكلى ولا جزئي اللهم الا ان يراد بالكلى ما لا يكون كليا بالفعل بل من شأنه ان يكون كليا بالفعل أم لا وكذا الجزئي .
نعم يمكن دفعه بان الصورة الذهنية كما تطلق على كيفية تحصل في العقل مرآة لمشاهدة ذي الصورة ، يطلق أيضا على الماهية المعلومة المتميزة بواسطة تلك الصورة في الذهن باعتبار حصولها في الذهن ووجودها الذهني والمنقسم إلى الكلى الذي لا يمتنع فرض صدقه على كثيرين وإلى الجزئي الذي يمتنع فرض صدقه عليه هو المعنى الثاني . ( شيخ عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
On the words ‘Know that what is understood from an expression …’: the apparent implication is that a concept (mafhūm) and a meaning (maʿnā) are identical in themselves. A meaning, according to the definition given, is the mental form considered insofar as an expression has been assigned to it. A concept would therefore also be a mental form. It would follow that universality and particularity are attributes of the form, although they are attributes of what the form represents. It would also follow that, in distinguishing universal from particular, what matters is whether conceiving the form prevents [its being predicated of many] or does not prevent it, whereas what matters is whether conceiving what it represents prevents this or does not.

This difficulty is not removed by the investigator al-Sharīf’s remark in his marginalia on the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ. After the commentator’s words ‘a concept is what occurs in the intellect,’ he says that ‘what occurs’ means what is of a kind to occur in the intellect, whether or not it actually occurs. For the thing of a kind to be present in the mind is the form, not what the form represents. Moreover, ‘what occurs’ means what actually occurs, since universality and particularity are mental attributes: what has not actually occurred in the mind is neither universal nor particular. Unless, that is, ‘universal’ is taken to mean what need not actually be universal but is of a kind to be universal, whether actually so or not; the same would apply to ‘particular.’

The difficulty can, however, be removed as follows. ‘Mental form’ is used both for a quality occurring in the intellect which serves as a mirror for apprehending what the form represents, and for the known quiddity distinguished in the mind by means of that form, considered with respect to its presence in the mind and its mental existence. It is the latter that is divided into a universal, whose predication of many can be supposed without impossibility, and a particular, whose predication of many cannot be so supposed.
records.editorial: Supersedes the Stage112 partial English, which remains in its immutable source file. This is full coverage of the digital numbered note, not a photographed witness. The digital wording ‘سواء حصل بالعقل أولا’ and the repeated potential/actual phrasing are retained in Arabic; the English reads the evident contrast ‘whether or not it occurs.’ The distinction is between a particular cognitive quality and the represented quiddity considered in mental existence; it does not establish that every school uses ‘mental form’ identically.
records.revision: Stage113 full digital Arabic and consecutive English; no photo/manuscript certification

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فإن المعنى اما مفعل من عنى
records.english: The word *maʿnā* can be derived as a noun from the verb “to intend,” or as a lightened passive-participial form meaning what is intended. The first derivation is preferred because it avoids assuming several sound changes and deletions required by the second.
records.editorial: Traditional morphological derivation, not independent comparative etymology.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, followed by separate ʿAbd al-Raḥīm note
records.arabicLemma: قوله الفرض هاهنا بمعنى تجويز العقل
records.english:
The division of conceptions into universal and particular is stated in terms of whether the intellect can **allow** the concept's application to many. If “supposition” merely meant arbitrarily imagining a different arrangement of things, one might imagine even Zayd as distributed among several individuals, making every individual concept universal. Instead *farḍ* here means a possibility the intellect accepts under the content's nature, not whatever words a speaker happens to entertain.

Several familiar objections follow. A distant figure might be thought to be Zayd or ʿAmr or Bakr; does that make the seen individual universal? The answer distinguishes application to many *jointly* from uncertainty over which **one** of many is indicated. The remote figure has one actual intended referent, although the observer has several alternative conjectures. Conversely a general concept with no external instances, such as the supposed partner of God or the phoenix, need not become particular merely through lacking instantiation.

A second objection concerns the phrase “to many” (*kathīrīn*), with its masculine rational plural. If it strictly excluded nonrational referents, concepts of animals or nonliving things could not be universal, an absurd consequence. A semantic rather than school-grammar reading is therefore preferred; some propose “to multiplicity” (*ʿalā al-kathra*) instead. Another objection concerns the minimum number denoted by “many,” but a universal's potential applicability does not become particular because only two or five instances happen to be available in some imagined domain.
records.editorial: Q216–218 long source, several objections/replies omitted, hence PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm with further quoted Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī intervention
records.arabicLemma: قوله كشريك الباري تعالى
records.english:
A concept like “a partner of the Creator” can be universal in form while having no real instances. The immediate objection is that rational consideration judges the actual instantiation of such a thing impossible, so how can one claim that the intellect allows many instances? The reply distinguishes **mere initial intelligibility of a general concept** from a subsequent demonstration of impossibility. The mind can combine the descriptive elements before proving that no such instance exists.

The source then tests concepts such as “not-thing,” “nonexistent” and “impossible under general possibility.” It distinguishes supposing an impossible situation from asserting that the supposed situation can in fact occur. However, this approach risks allowing the arbitrary supposition that a personal individual has many instances. To exclude that, the writer says a definite individual cannot be multiplied under precisely the very individuality in question, whereas a universal description may remain repeatable in a merely assumed domain.
records.editorial: Extended dispute crosses Q218–219, important distinctions of abstract repeatability vs real possibility; not fully translated, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mullā ʿAlī Akbar al-Ahrī, independently signed
records.arabicLemma: قوله أي لم يمتنع
records.english:
The expression “it does not prevent” may concern general possibility—removing necessity from one side—rather than special possibility—removing necessity from both existence and nonexistence. The text distinguishes the necessary, the impossible and the specially possible through which side's necessity is excluded. An objection says that, if the concept of possible instances uses general possibility in one sense, it may include the impossible; if it uses special possibility, it cannot properly be contrasted with what is necessary.

The response fixes the side under discussion. Removing the necessity of *nonexistence* allows both what is necessary and what is contingent but not what is impossible. Removing the necessity of existence, by contrast, can include the impossible. Since the intended alternative is to what is absolutely impossible, the former interpretation is preferred.
records.editorial: Separate signed al-Ahrī note, not automatically Y or other later scholar. A complex modal passage, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb p.25 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله أي لم تمتنع أفراده في الخارج
records.english: The intellect does not reject an instance's appearing in external reality. Under that preliminary condition, either one instance must exist while the rest cannot, or instances may remain possible whether or not actually present. The writer suggests it would be clearer to divide the cases explicitly into universally impossible, one necessary instance, and the different possible patterns, rather than relying on an ambiguous “or they are possible.”
records.editorial: Clarifies the classification of universal concepts by possible instance numbers.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: هو بالفتح طائر عظيم معروف الاسم
records.english: The *ʿanqāʾ* is described in a cited lexicon as a fabulous bird known by name but without an identifiable bodily specimen. A reported folk explanation connects its name with a white marking on the neck.
records.editorial: Folkloric lexicography; not a zoological assertion about an existing animal.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: قوله أو امتناعه كمفهوم واجب الوجود
records.english:
The concept “necessary existent” is universal as a concept even though sound metaphysical reasoning excludes the presence of more than one such existent. The text distinguishes what the mind can provisionally conceive under the words from what can be judged possible after proof. Otherwise the concept would be rendered particular by an external result of metaphysical demonstration rather than by its own abstract representational form.

A further objection says that the class of universals with possible instances should not contain a concept which, at most, could have only one instance. The reply distinguishes impossibility at the first apprehension from impossibility after analysis and considers whether a plural expression of “instances” may stand generically for a single or several individuals. The same argument cannot simply infer that God has more than one real instantiation; it is a dispute over the classification of concepts, not a metaphysical declaration.
records.editorial: Long Q220 source, several scope replies; PARTIAL.

records.speaker: al-Taqrīb pp.25 (quoted)
records.arabicLemma: قوله كمعلومات الباري
records.english:
The things known by God can be considered without limit in number, on the cited philosophical account. The source also mentions rational souls under a theory of an eternal succession of events. “Without end” in the latter case does not mean that there must be a presently existing infinite aggregate of souls at a single instant; it means that after any one soul there may be another without reaching a last soul. The distinction between an actual simultaneous infinity and an unending succession matters to the argument.

The philosophical background presupposes doctrines about the eternity of the world and the soul which other theological schools deny. The source's words are descriptive of that position, not the editor's conclusion or a proof of an actual infinity.
records.editorial: Crosses Q220→221; some exact quoted tradition and constraints remain unverified, PARTIAL.

records.speaker: Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī
records.arabicLemma: فانهم قالوا بان العالم قديم لا أول له
records.english: Those philosophers are reported to hold that the world has neither a first moment nor a last, and that rational souls can continue successively without final bound. This is a potential unending numerical succession, not a demand that every possible soul exist concurrently. The note compares it with the indefinitely continuing number sequence and the unlimited objects of divine knowledge.
records.editorial: Reports the philosophers' cosmological account, not an independently proven historical consensus.

records.speaker: Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (source signature)
records.arabicLemma: قوله : « اى كل كليين »
records.arabicFullText:
قوله : « اى كل كليين » : يعنى ان اللام في قوله : « والكليان » للاستغراق ، فيعم جميع الكليات وفيه ان الكلام انما في الكليات التي لها مصداق في الخارج كما سنشير اليه .
ثم انما اعتبر النسب الأربع بين الكليين ولم يعتبر بين المفهومين ، لان المفهومين اما كليان أو جزئيان أو كلى وجزئي ، فلو قال : « المفهومان » لربما يتوهم جريان جميع اقسام النسب في كل واحد من الأقسام الثلاثة وليس كذلك بل انما يتحقق بين الكليين بمعنى انه يوجد كليان مخصوصان بينهما تباينا وكليان آخران بينهما تساو وهكذا .
واما الجزئيان فلا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين واما الجزئي والكلى فلا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين والعموم مطلقا ، لان الجزئي ان كان جزئيا لهذا الكلى فيكون أخص منه مطلقا وان لم يكن جزئيا له فيكون مباينا ، فلما قال : « الكليان » علم أن ليس حال القسمين الأخيرين كذلك هكذا يستفاد من كلام بعضهم . والحق ان وجه التخصيص ، الإشارة إلى أن المقصود الأصلي معرفة أحوال نسب الكليات بعضها مع بعض .
وما ذكر ان الجزئيين لا يتحقق بينهما الا التباين ، فيه انه ان أريد به ان التباين بينهما باعتبار التصادق كما هو الحق فلا نسلم انهما متباينان وكيف ، ومرجع التباين كما سيذكره المحشى ، إلى سالبتين كليتين والسالبتان الحاصلتان من الجزئيين شخصيتان وعلى هذا قس الكلى والجزئي ، وان أريد به ان التباين أعم من أن يكونا باعتبار التصادق أو باعتبار الموجود فلا نسلم ان الجزئيين لا يكونان إلا متباينين فان النسب الأربع ح تجرى بينهما وبين الكلى والجزئي . ( عبد الرحيم )
records.english:
On ‘that is, any two universals’: the definite article in ‘the two universals’ is exhaustive and therefore embraces all universals. There is a difficulty: the discussion concerns only universals having an instance in external reality, as we shall indicate.

The four relations were considered between two universals, rather than between two concepts, because two concepts may both be universal, both particular, or one universal and the other particular. Had the author said ‘the two concepts,’ one might suppose that every kind of relation occurs within each of these three classes. That is not so. All four occur between universals in the sense that there are two particular universals between which disjointness obtains, two others between which equality obtains, and so forth.

Between two particulars, on this explanation, only disjointness occurs. Between a particular and a universal, only disjointness or unrestricted inclusion occurs: if the particular is an instance of this universal, it is absolutely narrower than it; if it is not an instance, it is disjoint. By saying ‘the two universals,’ the author indicates that the other two classes are not in the same position. This is what can be gathered from some writers. The truth, however, is that the restriction indicates that the principal purpose is to learn the relations of universals to one another.

As for the assertion that only disjointness occurs between two particulars: if the disjointness concerns their joint predicability, as it properly should, we do not grant that they are disjoint in this technical sense. How could we? Disjointness, as the glossator will state, resolves into two universal negatives; but the two negatives formed from particulars are singular propositions.
